hyde: Any statute or portion thereof inconsistent with these rules is superseded to the extent of the inconsistency. Statutory provisions not addressed by these rules remain in full force and effect unless expressly repealed. The court shall apply statutory procedures where no rule governs, provided such application does not conflict with the intent or explicit language of these rules.

These rules shall be construed to secure the just, speedy, and inexpensive determination of every action. No error or defect in procedure or form shall invalidate any proceeding unless a party objects promptly and substantial prejudice results from the failure to comply with the rule. The court may disregard technical errors that do not affect substantial rights.

A case pending when these rules take effect shall be conducted under former rules unless the court orders otherwise. On motion by any party or sua sponte, the court may order that a pending case proceed under these rules if justice requires. The court’s determination is final and not subject to appeal.

Unless the court orders otherwise, singular terms include the plural and plural terms include the singular. A reference to a party includes all parties joined in the action. A reference to an affidavit includes multiple affidavits filed by any party. Gender references are interchangeable. This interpretation applies to all rules unless the context clearly requires a different meaning.

When the period of time prescribed or allowed is less than seven days, intermediate Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays shall be excluded in the computation. If the last day falls on a Saturday, Sunday, or legal holiday, the period continues until the end of the next day which is not a Saturday, Sunday, or legal holiday. The day of the act, event, or default from which the designated period begins to run is not included.

All documents filed electronically or generated by the court within the case management system constitute the official record of the proceeding. No paper counterpart is required for such documents to be part of the record. The court shall maintain these electronic records as the exclusive source for all filings and orders, unless a specific rule mandates physical preservation.

Discovery materials lodged with the clerk shall constitute part of the official court record. A party may move to strike such materials from the record for good cause shown. Unless otherwise ordered by the court, all filed discovery documents remain subject to public inspection and retention requirements applicable to other pleadings and papers on file.

The court record includes all documents filed with the clerk and all recordings made by the court. Information generated by the court’s case management and electronic filing systems is not part of the court record unless specifically incorporated by order. A party may move to include such system-generated information in the record on motion, showing good cause. The court shall rule on such motion within 14 days.

A party seeking specific pronoun usage or form of address shall state such preferences in the caption of any filed pleading. Upon motion, the court shall honor stated preferences in open court proceedings, provided the request is reasonable and does not disrupt judicial administration. Failure to include preferences in the caption waives the right to compel their use during hearings.

In every juvenile proceeding, the caption must include the phrase “Juvenile Proceeding” immediately following the case number. This designation is mandatory regardless of whether the action arises under the Juvenile Code or other statutes governing minors. Failure to include this identifier does not invalidate the filing but requires immediate correction upon notice by the court clerk.

The clerk shall redact Social Security numbers from all documents before providing copies to the public, including certified copies. This requirement applies regardless of the filing date or document type. Failure to redact constitutes a violation of privacy protections. Parties may move to unseal specific information only upon showing good cause.

Confidential data submitted on separate sheets shall be used solely for case identification and administrative purposes. Such data must not appear in chronological entries or public records. Court staff may not disclose, release, or use these identifiers for any purpose other than maintaining the integrity of the court’s internal filing system, unless expressly authorized by law or court order.

Before issuing a register of actions containing dates of birth, the clerk must verify that the requester is listed on the current state-approved roster for accessing such information. The clerk shall confirm the requester’s identity and authorization status prior to release. If the requester is not verified as authorized, the clerk must withhold the date of birth from the document provided.

On motion or sua sponte, the court shall order redaction of personal data identifiers from documents filed with the court. A party must file a redacted copy within 14 days after filing an unredacted document. The original document remains part of the record but is sealed from public inspection. Failure to comply may result in sanctions.

A party filing a document containing a redacted protected identifier must file a corresponding index listing the full identifier with the clerk within ten days of filing the redacted document. The index shall be filed under seal and is not part of the public record. Failure to file the index may result in sanctions or dismissal of the related pleading.

If a prior action involving the same parties and issues is pending in another county, the complaint must include a case-initiation statement identifying that action by its docket number and the name of the presiding judge. Failure to include this information constitutes a defect in pleading subject to correction by leave of court or dismissal for failure to state a claim upon which relief can be granted.

The clerk of court shall maintain all electronically filed documents in digital format. The clerk must preserve these records in accordance with standards established by the State Court Administrative Office. Local rules regarding specific storage media or retention periods are prohibited unless expressly authorized by administrative order. Failure to comply mandates immediate correction upon notice from the administrative office.

Unless the State Court Administrator designates electronic filing as mandatory for a specific court or case type, parties may file documents electronically. A self-represented litigant is not required to use the system unless such designation applies. If designated mandatory, all filings shall be submitted electronically within the time prescribed by law, subject to exceptions granted by the court for good cause shown.

Unless the court orders otherwise, all filings shall be made electronically. A party seeking exemption from mandatory electronic filing must file a motion demonstrating inability to comply due to lack of access to technology or other good cause. The court may grant leave to file on paper if it finds that requiring electronic filing would impose an undue hardship.

A document filed electronically is deemed filed at the date and time shown on the confirmation of transmission received by the filer, regardless of when the clerk reviews it. This rule applies whether filing fees are paid or waived. If the electronic system is unavailable, a party may file manually with the clerk during business hours.

A party serving documents electronically must use the court’s electronic filing system. If an opposing party has not registered with the system, the serving party shall serve that party by traditional means. Service is complete upon mailing or delivery. The serving party must file a certificate of service stating the method used and confirming compliance with this rule within three days after service.

Service by electronic transmission through the court’s e-filing system constitutes service upon counsel of record. No separate proof of service is required unless the court orders otherwise or a party demonstrates that service failed. Service is complete upon transmission, provided the recipient has access to the system. A party may request alternative service methods if electronic delivery is impracticable.

If electronic filing is unavailable due to system failure, the court shall post notice of the outage and any deadline extension on its website. A party must file within three days after service resumes if the original deadline falls during the outage. Failure to provide timely notice does not extend deadlines unless the court orders otherwise on motion showing good cause.

Unless the court orders otherwise at sentencing, all fines, penalties, and costs imposed shall be due and payable immediately upon entry of the judgment or order of disposition. Payment must be made to the clerk of the court within thirty days after the imposition of sentence, unless a different payment schedule is established by written agreement approved by the court.

An interpreter registered at the lower tier must have passed the oral portion of the certification examination within three years preceding the date of assignment. Failure to meet this requirement renders the registration invalid for court proceedings unless the court grants a specific waiver based on demonstrated necessity and lack of available certified interpreters.

An interpreter must be certified by the State Court Administrative Office or appear on the court’s approved list. Qualification depends solely on individual certification status, not employment arrangement. Whether an interpreter is retained directly or through an agency is immaterial to qualification. Agencies are not required to be listed; only the specific interpreter assigned to the proceeding must meet statutory certification requirements.

The court shall order a party who received court-appointed interpretation services to reimburse the county within thirty days after final disposition if the party had the financial ability to pay for such services at the time of appointment. Reimbursement is mandatory regardless of whether the proceeding is civil or criminal, provided the party’s financial status was determined sufficient to bear the cost.

On motion, the district court shall review the trial court’s denial of an interpreter de novo. The reviewing panel must determine whether the denial violated the defendant’s right to due process. No deference is owed to the initial ruling. The decision shall be final and binding upon all parties within thirty days of filing.

A pro se prisoner’s filing is timely if deposited in the facility’s internal mail system before the deadline. The court shall accept a sworn declaration by the prisoner, stating the date of deposit, as prima facie evidence of timely filing. The opposing party may rebut this presumption only by clear and convincing evidence that the filing was not deposited within the prescribed time.

The Supreme Court shall transmit proposed rule changes to the State Bar Association and other interested entities at least ninety days before adoption. Proposals and comment deadlines must be published in the Michigan Courts website and the official state register. Interested persons may submit written comments within the specified period. The Court shall consider all comments before finalizing amendments.

A fee waiver granted in one civil action does not apply to any other pending or future proceeding. In each separate case, a party seeking relief from fees must file a new application with the court. The court shall determine eligibility based on current financial circumstances and may require updated documentation. Approval in prior matters is not binding upon the court for subsequent filings.

A waiver of fees granted by the trial court does not extend to proceedings in the Court of Appeals. A party seeking fee relief on appeal must file a motion with the appellate court within fourteen days after filing the notice of appeal. The appellate court shall determine the request based on the merits and applicable standards, independent of the trial court’s prior determination.

Upon granting an application for waiver of costs, the clerk shall issue a written order specifying the waived fees. This order constitutes part of the official court record and shall be filed with the case documents. Any party or member of the public inspecting the file may view the order. The clerk must provide a copy of the order to the applicant within ten days of entry.

Upon denial of an application for waiver of fees or costs, the court shall state its reasons in writing. If the applicant moves for reconsideration and the motion is denied, the court shall include specific findings supporting the denial in the order. Failure to provide written reasons constitutes grounds for immediate review.

On motion of any party, the court shall remove a judge if personal animus toward counsel exists. The motion must be filed within ten days after the party becomes aware of the grounds for removal. The court may deny the motion if the alleged hostility is directed solely at counsel and does not affect the fairness of the proceedings or the rights of the parties involved in the case.

Upon granting disqualification, the presiding judge shall reassign the case to another qualified circuit judge within ten days. If no other judge is available or qualified, the presiding judge may designate a special judge from the district court or request assignment from the Administrative Office of the Courts, ensuring continuity and impartial adjudication without undue delay.

Upon disqualification of a business court judge, the case remains in the business court division. If no other business court judge is available, the Chief Judge of the circuit court shall assign a replacement judge within ten days. The assigned judge must be familiar with commercial litigation matters. A party may move for reassignment only upon showing cause.

Service upon a limited liability company shall be made by delivering a copy of the process to an officer, managing member, or agent authorized by appointment or law to receive service. If no such person is available, service may be made by leaving copies at the principal place of business with a person in charge.

On motion showing reasonable diligence in attempting service by prescribed methods, the court may order service by any other method reasonably calculated to give notice. The motion must be supported by an affidavit or verified statement setting forth facts demonstrating such diligence. The supporting affidavit or statement must be sworn to or verified within ten days before filing the motion.

On motion filed within 14 days after service of a pleading or other paper, a party may move to dismiss for defective service. The court shall not dismiss an action solely because the method of delivery did not strictly comply with these rules if the opposing party received actual notice and was not prejudiced by the defect. Substantial compliance satisfies the requirement.

Upon filing a limited appearance, counsel shall serve all subsequent pleadings, motions, and notices upon the appearing attorney rather than the self-represented party, except for documents requiring personal service under this rule. Service upon counsel satisfies requirements for notice to the represented party regarding matters within the scope of the limited appearance.

A stipulation for service by electronic means must specify the e-mail address for each party or attorney. The designated address shall correspond to the contact information previously filed with the court or contained in a pleading. A party may amend this designation by filing a notice of change within three days of the modification, ensuring all subsequent notices are directed to the updated address on file.

If electronically served documents are rejected by the recipient’s system, service is ineffective. The serving party must promptly serve the document by an alternative method permitted under this rule. Proof of such alternative service constitutes proof of service. Failure to effect timely service does not extend any deadline unless the court orders otherwise on motion showing good cause.

A party asserting that a claim is barred by an arbitration agreement shall file a motion to compel arbitration within seven days after service of the pleading raising the claim. The court may stay proceedings pending resolution of the motion. Failure to timely move constitutes waiver of the right to arbitrate, unless excused for good cause shown.

A party asserting fraud, mistake, or misrepresentation in an insurance application shall state with particularity the circumstances constituting the defense. A general denial is insufficient to raise such affirmative defenses. Failure to plead these matters specifically waives their assertion unless the court permits amendment for good cause shown within the time prescribed by this rule.

A party asserting an affirmative defense of third-party liability shall file a statement identifying such person within twenty-one days after serving its answer. If facts supporting the defense are discovered later, the court may, on motion and for good cause shown, permit amendment or supplementation of the statement to include the additional information, provided no prejudice results to opposing parties.

A party pleading a written instrument must attach a copy to the complaint unless the instrument is in the possession of an adverse party or third person, unavailable through reasonable diligence, or already filed with a public office. If not attached, the pleading must state the reason and describe the instrument with sufficient particularity to identify it.

The court shall schedule a hearing on the motion within thirty days of filing. If the court orders discovery specifically related to the merits of the motion, the thirty-day period is tolled during the pendency of such discovery and resumes upon completion. The court may extend the time for good cause shown.

Unless local administrative order provides otherwise, a party filing a dispositive motion in a non-electronic court shall serve one additional copy of the brief and supporting affidavits directly to chambers. This copy must be clearly marked “Chambers Copy” on the cover page and filed within three days after service upon opposing counsel.

On motion asserting a defense of limitations, if genuine issues of material fact exist, the court may try those issues without a jury. A demand for jury trial does not preclude this procedure. The court shall determine factual disputes necessary to resolve the defense before proceeding to other matters.

On partial disposition of claims, the court shall order an entry of judgment on the disposed claims unless it expressly directs otherwise to avoid injustice or facilitate efficient resolution. The action shall proceed with respect to the remaining claims. A party may move for a new trial or amend pleadings regarding the surviving counts within the time prescribed by these rules.

A party filing a motion shall file supporting briefs simultaneously. The combined length of the motion and brief must not exceed twenty pages, exclusive of exhibits, certificates of service, and tables of contents. Exhibits do not count toward this limit. The court may grant leave to file longer documents for good cause shown. Failure to comply may result in denial of the motion.

A party relying on a document in an affidavit shall attach it as an exhibit unless the document is not reasonably procurable by the affiant. If unattached, the affidavit must state that the document is unavailable and identify its custodian. The court may order production or strike the affidavit if the statement is insufficient or the document is accessible.

A party must serve an opposition brief no later than seven days before the hearing date. Service is complete upon delivery to opposing counsel or their attorney of record. If the last day for service falls on a Saturday, Sunday, or legal holiday, service may be made on the next business day. The court may shorten this time for good cause shown.

If a party does not appear at a scheduled hearing, that party must file a written statement of position with the court no later than five days before the hearing date. Failure to file such a statement constitutes consent to the entry of the proposed order or judgment as presented by the appearing party, unless the court orders otherwise for good cause shown.

A party seeking reconsideration must file a motion within fourteen days after entry of the order. The court may grant relief only if the moving party demonstrates that new evidence has come to light, or that the prior ruling was based on a clear error of law or fact not previously addressed. Mere reargument of points already considered shall not constitute grounds for reconsideration.

A party filing a proposed judgment or order for entry following settlement shall not be required to pay a motion fee. This exemption applies when the filing is accompanied by notice to all parties and does not require judicial determination of disputed issues. The clerk shall accept such filings without assessment of additional fees, provided the document conforms to formatting requirements and seeks only ministerial approval.

If a minor is served with process and no guardian ad litem has been appointed, any party may move for appointment within twenty-one days after service. The court shall appoint a guardian ad litem upon such motion unless the minor is represented by counsel who consents to act as guardian.

If a party dies after filing a statement of death, any party may move to substitute the proper parties within 90 days after service of the statement. If no motion for substitution is made within that time, the action shall be dismissed as to the deceased party. The court may extend the time for cause shown.

A party may implead a third person as an indemnitor without leave of court if the pleading is served within 14 days after serving the answer. If service occurs later, the party must obtain leave of court on motion showing good cause. The third person shall serve any responsive pleading within 21 days after service of the summons and complaint upon that person.

On motion by any party, the court may order separate trials of one or more issues, claims, cross-claims, counterclaims, or third-party claims if it determines that separation promotes convenience, avoids prejudice, or achieves economy of time and expense. The court shall issue such an order when joinder causes undue delay or confusion, ensuring efficient administration of justice without compromising the rights of any party involved in the proceeding.

If the filing fee is not paid within thirty days after transfer, the receiving court shall dismiss the action without prejudice. The clerk must notify all parties of the pending dismissal. A party may move to reinstate the case upon payment of the fee and costs, but failure to pay constitutes a waiver of the right to proceed in that venue.

Upon transfer for lack of venue, the transferring court shall assess a filing fee against the party who initiated the action in the improper county. This fee must be paid within fourteen days of the order. Failure to pay constitutes grounds for dismissal. The receiving court may, on motion and for good cause shown, award reasonable costs and attorney fees to the opposing party incurred by the improper venue selection.

On motion showing improper venue manipulation, the court shall transfer the action. The plaintiff must pay the new filing fee within fourteen days. The court may order the plaintiff to reimburse reasonable defense costs incurred solely due to the improper venue selection. Failure to pay fees or costs constitutes grounds for dismissal without prejudice.

If an order transferring a case fails to specify the statutory or rule authority for the transfer, the receiving clerk shall return the file within five days. The clerk must include a written notice identifying the deficiency and stating that acceptance is refused until proper authority is established. The sending court shall correct the order and resubmit the file in compliance with this rule.

In a first-party no-fault action, a plaintiff shall disclose, without request, all outstanding balances owed to treating providers. This disclosure must occur within thirty days of filing the complaint or upon discovery of new charges. Failure to provide this information may result in sanctions or dismissal of claims related to unpaid medical expenses.

A party claiming personal injury shall serve written requests for authorization to obtain medical records within thirty days after filing a complaint or answer. The requesting party must provide blank forms. The responding party shall execute and return such authorizations within twenty-one days. Failure to comply may result in sanctions, including preclusion of evidence regarding the claimed injuries.

A party shall serve initial disclosures within fourteen days after service of the first responsive pleading or first motion under Rule 2.110, unless otherwise ordered by the court. Disclosures need not be served on a party who has not yet appeared in the action. The court may order earlier disclosure or extend the time for good cause shown.

A party must serve mandatory disclosures within twenty-eight days after service of the pleading requiring a response. If no pleading requires a response, disclosures must be served within one hundred forty days after the complaint is served. A party may move for an extension or reduction of this time upon showing good cause.

A party shall produce all drafts of an expert’s report prepared by the expert or under the expert’s direction, regardless of form, including handwritten notes, audio recordings, or electronic files. No work-product protection applies to these materials. Production must occur with the final expert report or within ten days after a request for production.

On motion of any party or sua sponte, the court may order that a deposition be closed to all persons except those expressly permitted by the court. The order shall specify the conditions under which attendance is allowed. This authority applies regardless of whether the deposition is taken before trial or during discovery proceedings.

A party represented by counsel must sign all pleadings, motions, and responses to interrogatories. An unsigned document shall be stricken unless promptly signed after the omission is called to attention. A party not represented by counsel must sign every pleading, motion, or response in their own name. The signature constitutes a certification that the document has been read and is presented for proper purposes.

Each answer to an interrogatory shall be signed by the party or the party’s attorney. If an answer is not signed, it is deemed waived unless the omission is corrected within 14 days after service of a written notice of the defect. Failure to correct the defect within that time renders the answer ineffective and subject to striking by the court on motion.

A party serving initial disclosures shall certify that they are complete and correct as of the time of service. The certification does not warrant completeness for matters arising thereafter. A party must supplement disclosures to reflect information subsequently acquired or determined to be inaccurate, within thirty days after trial settings are established or upon learning of the omission or inaccuracy.

On motion showing probable cause that a witness is dying or may leave the state, the court shall order testimony preserved by deposition. The moving party must file an affidavit specifying the expected testimony and why it cannot be obtained after action commencement. The court may require security for costs. Deposition proceeds as in civil actions.

On motion showing that taking testimony in the ordinary manner is impractical due to the witness’s location outside the state, the court may order deposition by written interrogatories or video link. The moving party must file the motion at least 14 days before trial. The court shall specify the time, place, and manner of examination, ensuring substantial compliance with international treaty requirements where applicable.

Unless otherwise ordered by the court or agreed upon in writing by the parties, the reporter shall not prepare a transcript of the deposition. A party seeking a transcript must request it within 14 days after the deposition concludes. Upon such request, the reporter shall prepare and deliver the transcript within 30 days. Failure to timely request a transcript constitutes a waiver of the right to obtain one from the reporter at the requesting party’s expense.

If a deposition is recorded by audio means, it must be transcribed before use at trial or hearing. The party seeking to introduce the recording shall bear the cost of transcription unless the court orders otherwise on motion for good cause shown. The transcript must be filed within ten days after notice of intent to offer the evidence.

The officer shall administer the oath, transmit questions to the witness, and record answers. Upon completion, the officer shall certify compliance with this rule and seal the deposition in an envelope endorsed with the title of the action. The party requesting the deposition shall promptly file the certified deposition with the court or serve it on other parties as required by law.

Objections to deposition testimony on grounds of form, including leading or compound questions, must be made promptly during the examination. Failure to object at the deposition waives the objection unless substantial injustice would result if the error were not corrected. The court may permit withdrawal of a waiver for good cause shown.

A party producing electronically stored information shall provide it in a form reasonably usable by the requesting party. If the data exists solely in a proprietary system, the producing party must convert it to an ordinary format or provide reasonable access. Failure to do so constitutes non-compliance with discovery obligations, subject to court sanction.

A party served with discovery requests together with the summons and complaint shall serve a response within 60 days after service of the summons and complaint. A party served with discovery requests at any other time shall serve a response within 30 days after service of the request, unless the court orders otherwise on motion for good cause shown.

A party may introduce an abstract of title in lieu of producing original recorded documents to prove matters contained therein. This privilege applies only to records filed with the county register of deeds or clerk of the circuit court. The abstract must accurately reflect the contents of the original record. The court shall admit such abstracts unless a party objects on the ground that the abstract is inaccurate or incomplete.

A party may move to compel discovery if another party fails to answer interrogatories fully or evasively. The moving party need not await a formal refusal. On motion, the court shall order answers and may impose sanctions for noncompliance or evasion. Such motions must be filed within thirty days after service of the response or expiration of the time allowed for response.

On motion, the court may award reasonable attorney fees to a party who prevails on a motion to compel discovery if the opposing party’s conduct necessitated the motion. Fees shall not be awarded if the moving party unreasonably delayed filing the motion or if the opposing party promptly complied after receiving informal notice of the deficiency.

On motion filed within ten days after entry of judgment, the court shall award reasonable expenses, including attorney fees, incurred in proving a fact not admitted if the refusal to admit was unreasonable. The court may deny such award if the opposing party demonstrates that the refusal was based on good faith belief that the evidence would support their position or that the matter was genuinely in dispute.

The court clerk shall retain custody of filed video depositions. A party may request return of the recording on motion showing good cause. The court may order release to a designated custodian if security measures protect the integrity of the record. Unless otherwise ordered, the original recording remains in the courthouse until final disposition of the case.

Upon final disposition of an action, the clerk shall retain the record for two years. Thereafter, the clerk may destroy or return exhibits and transcripts to the parties unless a party files a written request for retention within thirty days after notice of expiration. Failure to file such a request constitutes consent to destruction or return without further order of the court.

The court shall address stipulations regarding document genuineness and facts at the initial pretrial conference. Parties must submit proposed stipulations within fourteen days of the conference date. Failure to stipulate constitutes a waiver of objection to authenticity, unless good cause is shown. The court may order further discovery if stipulations remain unresolved.

The court may limit the number of expert witnesses, order separate discovery for experts, and require written reports. On motion or sua sponte, the court shall issue an order setting these parameters within thirty days after the early scheduling conference. Parties must comply with such orders. Failure to comply may result in sanctions, including exclusion of testimony.

The court may issue a scheduling order without consultation. A party seeking to modify the order must file a written request within fourteen days of service. Failure to timely request amendment constitutes waiver of objections to the schedule’s terms. Thereafter, modification is permitted only upon a showing of good cause and manifest injustice. The court retains discretion to enforce or amend the order at any time.

Each party shall appear at the final pretrial conference through counsel who will conduct the trial. Substitution of counsel for this purpose is prohibited unless the court, on motion and for good cause shown, grants leave. Failure to comply may result in sanctions or dismissal.

Within ten days after the final pretrial conference, each party shall file a joint order setting forth all matters agreed upon. A defendant asserting affirmative claims against codefendants or third parties shall specify those claims and any defenses thereto. Failure to include such claims in the joint order constitutes a waiver of the right to assert them at trial, unless the court permits amendment for good cause shown.

Within fourteen days of the conference, parties shall identify all reasonably accessible electronic data repositories. The court may limit discovery to sources where the burden or expense of collection substantially outweighs likely benefit. Parties must stipulate to practical limitations on retrieval methods before seeking further orders regarding specific data sets.

Within 14 days after the conclusion of the electronic discovery conference, the parties shall file a written plan detailing their agreement regarding the scope, timing, and methods of electronic discovery. If the parties fail to agree on any matter, they shall state their disagreements in the plan. The court may modify the plan on motion or its own initiative.

A party seeking to appear by telephone at a scheduling conference must file a written request with the court at least five days before the scheduled date. The requesting party shall serve a copy of the request on all other parties. Appearance by telephone is permitted only if the court grants leave. Failure to provide timely notice may result in denial of the request.

If the parties stipulate to facilitative mediation, the process shall be completed within ninety days after the filing of the discovery plan. The court may extend this period for good cause shown on motion by a party. Failure to complete mediation within the prescribed time shall not preclude the court from ordering further proceedings or imposing sanctions as appropriate under these rules.

A party must serve a copy of the case evaluation summary on all other parties within three days after receipt from the evaluator. Service shall be made in accordance with the rules governing service of pleadings and papers in civil actions, unless the court orders otherwise for good cause shown. Failure to timely serve may result in sanctions or exclusion of the summary from consideration.

If all parties sign the case evaluation statement, judgment shall be entered against the party whose evaluation was less favorable to its opponent than that of the opposing party, unless the losing party pays the difference within ten days after the statement is filed. Failure to pay within this period results in automatic entry of judgment for the amount of the difference plus costs.

If an evaluation panel determines a defense frivolous, the defendant shall deposit security with the court within fourteen days after notice of the determination. Failure to deposit such security constitutes a waiver of the right to proceed on that defense. The court may extend this time for good cause shown, provided trial is not imminent.

If the defendant fails to pay the bond within twenty-one days after the panel’s determination that the defense is frivolous, the court shall enter a default judgment against the defendant for the plaintiff’s damages and costs. No further proceedings in the action shall be had, except as necessary to enforce the judgment or determine attorney fees.

Two or more circuit courts may establish and operate a joint case evaluation program by written agreement filed with the Administrative Office of the Courts. The agreement shall specify administrative procedures, cost allocation, and evaluator selection criteria. Participation is voluntary for parties unless otherwise ordered. The joint program must comply with all substantive requirements of this rule governing individual court programs.

A party accepting an offer of judgment must file a notice of acceptance with the court within ten days after service of the offer. Upon filing, the clerk shall enter judgment in accordance with the terms of the offer. If no notice is filed within the prescribed period, the offer is deemed withdrawn and may not be considered by the court unless the offering party consents to its revival.

The court shall consider community resources when establishing the ADR plan. Unless all parties agree in writing to select a specific mediator, the court may assign cases to approved community mediation centers. Party consent is required for any deviation from court-assigned providers. The plan must ensure access to qualified neutrals and comply with statutory requirements for alternative dispute resolution procedures.

The neutral mediator shall facilitate settlement discussions but may not impose a decision or bind the parties to any agreement. The mediator has no authority to determine liability, assess damages, or enter judgment. Any settlement reached must be voluntary and reduced to writing signed by all parties. The court retains exclusive jurisdiction over unresolved issues.

Upon conclusion of mediation, the mediator shall file a written report with the court within fourteen days stating whether settlement was reached. If no agreement is reached, the report shall state only that fact. The mediator shall not disclose any information regarding the substance of negotiations or positions taken by parties, except as otherwise provided by law or rule.

Unless the parties agree otherwise in writing, the mediator’s fees shall be shared equally by the parties. If no agreement exists, each party must pay one-half of the total cost within fourteen days after receipt of the invoice. The court may order an unequal allocation of fees on motion and for good cause shown.

The court shall maintain the mediator application file as confidential. No party or member of the public may inspect, copy, or disclose any portion of the file, including personal history, training records, or references. This restriction applies regardless of whether the mediation is in a commercial case. The court may release information only upon order for good cause shown.

Mediation communications are confidential and inadmissible in any civil action, including legal malpractice claims. A party may not introduce evidence of statements made during mediation to prove liability or defend against allegations. The court shall exclude such evidence on motion or sua sponte, regardless of whether the communication occurred before, during, or after settlement negotiations.

On motion, the court shall review mediation communications in camera to determine enforceability. A party may not introduce evidence of statements made during mediation proceedings. The court must exclude such evidence unless the settlement agreement is written, signed by all parties, and expressly states that it constitutes a binding contract. This rule applies regardless of any other law or rule regarding privilege or confidentiality.

Information disclosed during mediation remains confidential and inadmissible in any proceeding. This protection does not apply to statements made with intent to commit a crime or inflict bodily harm, nor to disclosures necessary to prevent imminent death or serious bodily injury. A party may disclose such information despite the confidentiality requirement.

Information disclosed in mediation remains confidential despite a mandatory abuse referral. The exception permitting that referral does not waive privilege for subsequent protective proceedings. Statements made during mediation shall not be admitted as evidence in any case arising from the referral, nor used to impeach a witness, unless all parties expressly consent in writing or disclosure is otherwise required by law.

Before approving settlement of a minor’s claim exceeding $30,000, the court shall order that proceeds be deposited in an interest-bearing account or trust. The check must be payable to the minor and the guardian ad litem jointly. Upon filing proof of deposit and a proposed order of dismissal, the judge may sign the dismissal without further hearing, provided no objection is filed within ten days.

A party issuing a subpoena to a nonparty for records shall serve a copy on every other party within three days after issuance. A nonparty may object to the subpoena by serving written objections on the party who issued it and that party’s attorney, if any, without filing a motion with the court.

Upon receipt of documents from a nonparty custodian, the clerk shall immediately notify all parties who issued the subpoena or order compelling production. Notification must occur within three days of receipt and may be made by electronic means or first-class mail. Failure to provide timely notice does not invalidate the production but may subject the clerk to sanctions for administrative delay upon motion by an affected party.

Opening statements shall be made before evidence is presented. The court may permit the defendant to defer its opening statement until immediately before presenting proof. On stipulation of all parties, the court may waive opening statements entirely. Failure to make an opening statement does not constitute a waiver of the right to do so unless the court orders otherwise.

The court shall establish standard procedures for counsel’s review of completed juror qualification forms. These procedures must specify the manner, timing, and conditions under which attorneys may examine the documents. The court may modify these standards on motion by a party or sua sponte to ensure fairness and efficiency in jury selection proceedings.

Upon completion of jury selection, juror questionnaires remain under court control. A party or counsel shall not disclose, disseminate, or provide copies of such questionnaires to any non-party, including consultants, without prior written order of the court. Unauthorized distribution constitutes a violation of local access procedures and may subject the offending party to sanctions.

A party’s unused peremptory challenges shall not be forfeited upon completion of that party’s selection round. Challenges remain available for subsequent rounds until all jurors are seated or waived. The court may order alternating selection procedures. Unused strikes do not transfer to opposing counsel unless expressly ordered by the court for good cause shown.

If the committee recommends against instruction on a point, the court shall not give such instruction unless it determines that failure to do so would result in a miscarriage of justice or misstatement of the law. Mere assistance to the jury is insufficient. The court must find that the omission prejudices substantial rights or distorts legal principles before deviating from the committee’s affirmative recommendation against instruction.

On motion of counsel, the court may permit another attorney to substitute for the trial counsel during jury deliberations if such substitution does not prejudice a party’s rights. The moving party must file notice within 24 hours of the jury’s retirement. The court shall approve the substitution only upon finding that adequate preparation has occurred and that continuity of representation is maintained.

A party must deliver exhibits to the clerk’s office at least two days before trial. Upon admission, evidence remains under the court’s control. The judge may return admitted exhibits to the offering party if no appeal is anticipated or if retention serves no judicial purpose. Parties shall not remove admitted evidence without leave of court.

The court may grant relief not expressly requested in the pleadings if such relief is within the issues raised by the pleadings or evidence presented at trial, provided that no party objects to the entry of judgment on such grounds before the close of all evidence. A party waives any objection to relief inconsistent with its pleadings by failing to raise it prior to the submission of the case for decision.

Upon stipulation of all counsel regarding the form of an order, the court shall sign the order without further hearing or argument, unless the court determines that the proposed order is not in compliance with applicable law or rules. The court may require modifications to ensure legal sufficiency before signing.

If the court determines that a proposed order does not accurately reflect its ruling, the court may require the parties to submit revised proposals. The court shall notify the parties of any deficiencies and specify a time for compliance. Failure to comply with such an order may result in sanctions or the entry of judgment based on the record.

On motion or stipulation, the court may dismiss an action with prejudice, subject to reinstatement upon defendant’s default of the payment plan. The order must specify the payment terms, default consequences, and reinstatement procedure. All parties shall sign the stipulation unless the court orders otherwise. Reinstatement requires a motion filed within thirty days of default.

Service upon a party represented by counsel must be directed to that counsel’s last known address of record. If counsel has withdrawn or is unavailable, service shall be made on the party at their last known address. Proof of service, including an affidavit detailing the manner and date of delivery, must be filed with the court within ten days after service is effected.

On motion for default judgment, the moving party shall serve a copy of the motion and notice of hearing on the defaulting party. Service must be made in accordance with the rules governing service of process. If the defaulting party has not appeared, service may be made by mail or other method authorized by law. The court shall not enter judgment until proof of such service is filed.

In an action for a liquidated amount, if the defendant defaults, the clerk shall enter judgment without judicial review if the claim does not exceed $25,000. If the claim exceeds $25,000, the plaintiff must file a motion with the court for entry of judgment. The clerk may not enter judgment exceeding this limit.

In an action for a sum certain, if the defendant is a minor and has not appeared, the clerk shall not enter judgment upon default without prior order of the court. The court may grant such order only after determining that service was proper and that entry of judgment serves the best interests of the minor.

A party seeking default judgment against a minor must serve process through the minor’s guardian ad litem or parent. If no guardian is appointed, the court shall appoint one before entering judgment. A defendant who is a minor does not waive defenses by failing to answer until properly represented. Judgment may not be entered against a minor solely for failure to plead unless the minor has been duly served and represented in accordance with this rule.

On motion for default judgment, the movant shall file an affidavit of service proving that process was served in accordance with this rule. If personal service is not established, the movant must demonstrate compliance with alternative methods authorized by law. The court may grant the judgment only upon satisfaction that proper notice was given to the defendant.

A motion to set aside a default judgment shall be filed within twenty-one days after entry of the judgment. If service was made by publication or mail, the time for filing is extended to sixty-nine days after entry. The court may grant relief only upon a showing of excusable neglect and a meritorious defense. Failure to file within the prescribed period renders the motion untimely and subject to denial.

On motion filed within twenty-one days after entry of the order, the court may amend or make a new order correcting an error of fact or law. A party aggrieved by a partial summary disposition must appeal immediately; failure to do so waives review unless the court grants leave for good cause shown. The pending claims remain subject to further proceedings.

A party seeking a new trial as an alternative to other post-trial relief must file a motion within ten days after entry of the order disposing of any other post-trial motion. Failure to file such a motion constitutes a waiver of the right to a new trial, except for grounds not then existing or known with reasonable diligence. The court may grant a new trial on its own initiative within twenty-eight days after entry of judgment.

On motion for new trial, the court shall grant relief when the verdict is against the great weight of the evidence. This basis applies where findings conflict with proof, distinct from awards influenced by passion or prejudice. A party must file such motion within fourteen days after entry of judgment. The court may deny the motion if the evidence supports the jury’s determination.

On motion for new trial based solely on excessive verdict, the court may condition denial upon the moving party’s acceptance of a reduced amount. The party must accept the reduction within ten days after entry of the order. Failure to accept constitutes a waiver of the right to a new trial and results in final judgment for the reduced amount.

On motion filed within 21 days after discovery of the fraud, the court may relieve a party from a final judgment if the failure to defend was caused by the adverse party’s fraud, misrepresentation, or other misconduct. The moving party must show that the misconduct prevented a fair trial and that the motion is made with reasonable diligence upon discovery of the grounds.

A party must serve a copy of the judgment on the clerk within fourteen days after entry. Service is stayed pending disposition of any motion for reconsideration filed by another party. Upon expiration of the stay or denial of the motion, the prevailing party shall deliver the judgment to the sheriff for execution.

Upon satisfaction of a judgment, the prevailing party shall file a certificate of satisfaction with the clerk within fourteen days. The certificate must be signed by the judgment creditor or the creditor’s attorney of record. Filing constitutes notice to all parties that the judgment is satisfied. Failure to file does not invalidate the satisfaction but may preclude enforcement actions.

If no party files an objection within fourteen days after service of the motion for appointment of a receiver, the court may appoint the proposed receiver without further hearing. The court shall enter an order of appointment upon finding that the proposed receiver is qualified and that the appointment serves the interests of justice.

A person holding a note against the debtor is disqualified from appointment as receiver if such interest creates a conflict with fiduciary duties. On motion by any party, the court shall deny appointment unless the proposed receiver demonstrates that the conflict is immaterial and will not impair impartial administration of the estate. The moving party must file objections within fourteen days after notice of nomination.

On motion by any party, the court shall disqualify a proposed receiver who lacks neutrality due to personal or financial ties to the disputed property. A person who is not a creditor or former officer may be appointed only if free from conflicts of interest that impair impartiality. The objection must be filed within ten days after notice of appointment.

A party seeking reimbursement for paralegal services shall itemize hours devoted to substantive legal work. Such services must be performed under the direct supervision of an attorney. The paralegal must possess appropriate education, training, or experience. The court may allow reasonable compensation based on prevailing market rates, provided the work would otherwise have been performed by an attorney.

Upon the disability of the trial judge after verdict but before judgment, any other judge of the court may perform post-verdict duties. This authority applies only if the successor judge has reviewed the record sufficiently to ensure fairness. A party seeking substitution must file a motion within ten days of the disability. The successor judge shall issue final judgment or order accordingly.

These rules govern special proceedings in all courts of this state. They supplement the general civil rules. To the extent these rules do not address a particular matter, the general civil rules apply. A court may adopt local rules consistent with these provisions. Parties must comply with both sets of rules unless expressly excluded.

When multiple writs of execution are issued against the same debtor’s earnings, the employer shall withhold funds for each writ in the order received. If the total withholding exceeds statutory limits, the employer shall apply available earnings to the earliest-dated writ first. Remaining funds shall be applied to subsequent writs pro rata or in chronological order, as directed by the court.

The writ shall notify the defendant of the right to move for relief from the garnishment. The defendant must file such motion within ten days after service of the writ. Failure to file a timely motion constitutes a waiver of objections to the pre-judgment garnishment, and the court may order immediate turnover of funds upon expiration of the period.

Upon seizure of personal property under a writ of attachment, the sheriff shall cause the property to be appraised by two disinterested persons appointed by the court. The appraisers must sign an affidavit stating their valuation and file it with the clerk within 14 days after appointment. If either appraiser fails to act, the sheriff shall appoint another.

If the property is not found, the officer shall seize other defendant property of sufficient value to satisfy the judgment. The officer must provide a receipt for seized items. If the substituted property’s value exceeds the judgment amount, the officer shall return the excess proceeds to the defendant upon satisfaction of the debt and costs.

The chief judge shall maintain a current roster of authorized court officers and bailiffs. Within ten days after any change in personnel, the chief judge must submit an updated roster to the Administrative Office of the Courts. The Administrative Office shall not recognize any individual as a court officer or bailiff unless that person’s name appears on the most recently submitted roster.

Upon receipt of a registration packet containing an out-of-state support order, the clerk shall file the documents and assign a case number. Registration constitutes the commencement of a proceeding for enforcement purposes. No complaint is required to open the case. The court shall notify all parties of the registration within ten days.

The clerk may update a party’s address of record upon receipt of returned mail or written notice from any party. No motion is required for such administrative correction. If a party objects to the updated address, that party must file a motion to correct the record within fourteen days after receiving notice of the change. The court shall rule on any such motion promptly.

The court shall transmit copies of all pleadings, orders, and judgments to the earlier court within ten days of filing or entry. Such documents must be directed to the judge assigned to the pending proceeding in the earlier court. If no specific judge is identified, transmission shall be made to the clerk of that court for appropriate distribution.

Upon entry of an order affecting custody or guardianship, the prevailing party shall file a certified copy with the probate court having jurisdiction over the minor within fourteen days. This duty applies regardless of whether the probate court has issued a prior order or request. Failure to file may result in sanctions. The circuit court clerk shall notify parties of this requirement at the time of entry.

A party filing a custody complaint shall list all related cases, including neglect and support matters, pending in the same family division. This list must be served on opposing counsel simultaneously with the complaint. Failure to disclose related cases may result in sanctions or dismissal of the action upon motion by any party.

In an action for divorce, the complaint must state that irreconcilable differences have worked to destroy the marriage. Specific facts constituting the cause of action need not be pleaded. The court shall grant relief if the pleading contains sufficient factual allegations to establish jurisdiction and standing, regardless of the detail provided regarding the breakdown of the marital relationship.

On motion of any party, the court may dismiss an action for support if the parties reconcile or agree to terminate proceedings. Such motion must be filed within thirty days after the occurrence giving rise to the dismissal. The court shall grant the motion unless it finds that continuing the action serves the best interests of the child or public policy requires otherwise, regardless of whether a final judgment has entered.

The judgment of divorce controls over any separate support form regarding conflicting monetary awards. Both the judgment and the separate support order must bear the judge’s signature to be effective. If a discrepancy exists between signed documents, the court shall resolve the conflict on motion by either party within thirty days of entry.

Upon transfer of a support case to the court that entered the earlier order, the transferring court shall transmit the court file and Friend of the Court file within ten days. Transmission may be made by regular mail unless the receiving court orders otherwise or local rules require certified delivery. The files must include all pending motions and current financial information.

A party objecting to the referee’s findings must file specific objections within fourteen days after service of the referee’s report. Failure to file timely objections constitutes a waiver of the right to appeal or seek further review. The court shall consider only those matters specifically objected to, unless the court, on its own motion, determines that additional issues require de novo review.

A person serving as a mediator in a domestic relations action must complete a court-approved training course covering mediation skills and family law issues. The certificate of completion shall be filed with the clerk of the court within thirty days after the first mediation session. Failure to file proof of compliance constitutes grounds for removal from the case.

In domestic relations cases referred to mediation, the mediator shall administer a statewide screening instrument for intimate partner abuse prior to substantive discussions. The mediator may exercise professional judgment regarding the timing and manner of administration, provided that safety concerns are identified before joint sessions commence. Failure to screen does not invalidate subsequent agreements if no abuse is alleged.

The Friend of the Court shall withhold from disclosure any document received from a state agency expressly conditioned upon confidentiality. Such material remains exempt from production to opposing counsel or other parties, regardless of general file inspection rights. The office must maintain these records separately and return them to the originating agency if requested, ensuring strict adherence to the stipulated privacy terms.

A Friend of the Court Citizen Advisory Committee member seeking access to sealed materials shall file a written motion demonstrating good cause. The court may grant access only after determining that disclosure serves the best interests of the child and does not compromise safety or privacy. The court shall order specific conditions for viewing, copying, or retaining such materials.

The evaluator shall file the report with the court. Within seven days after filing, the court shall serve copies on all parties. Any party may file objections within fourteen days after service. The court may hold a hearing on the objections before ruling. The report is not admissible unless filed and served as provided herein.

Upon filing notice that collaborative practice has ended, the stay of proceedings is automatically lifted. No further motion or court order is required to resume litigation. Parties must proceed with the action in accordance with these rules. The court may schedule a status conference within thirty days if necessary to manage the docket.

In collaborative practice matters where parties file a joint petition for judgment without contest, no summons shall issue. Parties are not required to file separate answers or appearances. The court may enter judgment upon review of the joint petition and supporting documents, provided all statutory requirements for dissolution are satisfied and the agreement is in writing.

Upon filing of a consent judgment on the summary track, the clerk shall set a hearing within fourteen days. No pretrial conference is required. The court may shorten or extend these time limits for good cause shown. Parties must appear at the hearing unless excused by order. Failure to appear constitutes waiver of objections.

The notice to parties in an expedited consent judgment proceeding must state that either party may withdraw consent at any time prior to the entry of judgment. Upon such withdrawal, the action shall be scheduled for further proceedings or dismissed, as appropriate. Failure to include this warning renders the notice defective and subject to correction by the court on motion or sua sponte.

Upon filing a timely objection to mediation, proceedings shall be stayed pending judicial determination. The court may not order mediation or compel participation until it rules on the objection. If the court denies the objection, mediation shall proceed within fourteen days of the order. A party seeking immediate relief must file a motion showing good cause for bypassing this stay.

A party objecting to joint attendance at a Friend of the Court conference must file a written motion stating specific grounds for separation. The motion shall be filed no later than seven days prior to the scheduled conference date. Unless good cause is shown, the court may deny the request and order both parties to attend jointly. Failure to timely object waives the right to separate proceedings.

If settlement is not reached, the facilitator shall immediately file a report with the court stating the issues remaining unresolved. The facilitator may recommend specific judicial action or scheduling. No proposed order need be filed by the parties unless directed by the court. The court may proceed to hearing or further conferences based on the facilitator’s report without additional motion.

A party filing a psychological evaluation in a domestic relations action must clearly mark the document as confidential. The clerk shall file such documents separately from the public record. Unless the court orders otherwise, these materials remain non-public and are accessible only to parties, their counsel, and the court. Failure to flag the document does not waive its confidential status.

In summary support and paternity proceedings, if the proposed support amount is served with the complaint, any objection to the amount must be filed within twenty-one days after service of the complaint. Failure to file a timely objection constitutes consent to the proposed support order. The court may extend this period for good cause shown upon motion by a party.

Upon issuance of an order to show cause in a superintending control proceeding, the clerk shall immediately transmit a copy of the order to the respondent. Service of process is not required unless the court expressly orders otherwise. If separate service is ordered, it must be completed within seven days of the order’s entry.

The applicant shall file an affidavit setting forth specific facts showing immediate and irreparable injury if relief is denied. The order must state that it was issued without notice to the adverse party, specify the date and time of issuance, and describe the harm threatened. The court may require the applicant to post security.

On motion by the respondent, the court shall schedule an evidentiary hearing within seven days of service of the ex parte order. At such hearing, the petitioner bears the burden of proving that the restraining order should remain in effect to prevent immediate and irreparable harm. The court may modify or dissolve the order if the petitioner fails to meet this burden.

The master shall give notice of the hearing to all parties at least seven days before the date set. Each party may appear and be heard. If a party fails to appear after proper notice, the master may proceed in that party’s absence. The court may shorten or extend the time for notice on motion for good cause shown.

If the purchaser does not pay in cash, the court shall fix the time for payment of the purchase price, the manner of payment, and any security required. The order shall specify whether interest accrues on unpaid balances and the rate thereof. These terms must be established before confirmation of the sale to ensure adequate protection of the parties’ interests and compliance with statutory requirements governing partition proceedings.

Upon confirmation of sale, the clerk shall file a report specifying the property description, purchaser names, and purchase price for each lot. If partitioned property sold in separate lots, the report must detail the allocation of proceeds among co-owners according to their respective interests, subject to court approval within fourteen days after the sale date.

In a foreclosure action, the plaintiff shall identify all junior lienholders. Where more than five such interests exist, the plaintiff may describe them collectively by reference to a recorded instrument or public record index, rather than pleading each interest individually. Such collective description constitutes sufficient notice and satisfies the particularity requirement for joinder of necessary parties under this rule.

A party served with a cross-claim must serve an answer within twenty-one days after service of the pleading. If the cross-claim asserts liability to a third person, the party may move for leave to file a third-party complaint. Failure to respond constitutes a waiver of defenses and admits well-pleaded facts. The court may extend time on motion showing good cause.

On motion for class certification, the court shall weigh factors including the prospect of classwide injunctive or declaratory relief. A party seeking certification must demonstrate that such relief is appropriate and feasible. The court may consider whether individual claims predominate over common questions. This determination shall be made after hearing evidence and argument from all parties within thirty days of filing the motion.

On motion by a fiduciary seeking court approval for an act affecting numerous beneficiaries, the court shall order notice to all known beneficiaries or prescribe alternative notice reasonably calculated to inform interested parties. If individual notice is impracticable, the court may authorize publication or other substitute methods ensuring adequate protection of beneficiary interests before granting permission.

On motion of a party, the court shall vacate an arbitration award if the panel was induced to make the award by fraudulent means. A party must file such a motion within ninety days after the award is filed or delivered. Failure to file within this period waives the right to challenge the award on these grounds. The court may not modify the award based solely on alleged deception without vacating it entirely.

Upon imposition of a fine, the court shall issue an order to collect specifying the amount and debtor. The county treasurer must enforce collection within thirty days. If no execution is issued within six months, the treasurer shall certify the debt as uncollectible unless the court orders otherwise on motion.

Upon discharge from contempt proceedings where bond was posted, the court shall order immediate return of any unspent funds to the defendant. If the bond secured payment of fines or costs, the clerk shall deduct those amounts within ten days. Any remaining balance must be refunded without delay. The court may retain funds only to satisfy outstanding judgments or administrative fees expressly authorized by statute.

Upon judicial approval of reconstructed records, the copies shall constitute the official court file. They possess the same legal force and effect as the original documents for all purposes. No party may challenge the authenticity or validity of these approved substitutes in subsequent proceedings. The court retains discretion to order further verification if material discrepancies arise during litigation.

The hospital must file a motion for extension at least thirty days before the current order expires. Upon hearing, if the court finds continued confinement necessary to protect public health, it shall issue an amended commitment order. The new order may extend confinement for no more than six months from the date of issuance, subject to periodic review as required by law.

The clerk shall not disclose the existence or contents of a delayed birth registration file to any person unless authorized by court order. Access is restricted to parties with a demonstrated legal interest, upon motion showing good cause. The clerk must deny all other inquiries regarding the file’s status or location.

If a respondent is under eighteen years of age at the time the petition is filed, the court shall apply the juvenile subchapter procedures. The adult protection order subchapter does not govern proceedings involving minor respondents, regardless of the nature of the alleged conduct or the relief sought by the petitioner.

A party seeking protection from abuse shall disclose all prior domestic violence proceedings involving the parties, regardless of whether such cases are pending or closed. This disclosure must be made in writing within fourteen days of filing the petition. Failure to disclose prior adjudications may result in sanctions. The court may order additional discovery regarding criminal history if material to the safety determination.

Notwithstanding MCR 3.410(C)(2), if a respondent is a law enforcement officer required to carry a firearm, the court may, on motion, shorten the seven-day notice period for a hearing to modify or dissolve a personal protection order. The court shall set the hearing date and notify parties promptly to ensure public safety while preserving due process rights.

On motion for remote testimony, a party must file an affidavit stating the witness’s unavailability and proposed technology. Within three days, opposing counsel shall object in writing or consent. If no objection is filed, the court may order remote appearance. The court retains discretion to require personal attendance if credibility is at issue or technical reliability is insufficient.

A party may file a motion for relief from domestic violence in an existing domestic relations action without paying a separate filing fee. The motion shall specify the relief sought, including seizure of firearms. The court shall hear the motion promptly. If granted, the order shall be entered immediately and served upon the respondent. No additional case number is required if filed within the pending action.

The petitioner shall disclose in the complaint whether the respondent is employed as a peace officer or law enforcement personnel. This disclosure requirement applies regardless of the respondent’s specific title, agency affiliation, or certification status. Failure to disclose known employment as a peace officer constitutes noncompliance with this rule and may subject the petitioner to sanctions prescribed by the court.

A petitioner may withdraw an extreme risk petition before the court enters an order. The motion to withdraw shall be filed with the clerk and served on all parties. No filing fee is required for a motion to withdraw. Upon such motion, the court shall dismiss the petition without prejudice unless good cause exists to deny withdrawal.

The petitioner must establish that providing notice to the respondent before filing would create an immediate danger of serious physical harm to the respondent or others. Upon such showing, the court may issue an ex parte order without a hearing. The petitioner shall file supporting affidavits detailing the specific facts demonstrating this imminent risk within three days of filing the petition.

On motion showing probable cause that firearms remain in violation of an extreme risk order, the court shall issue a warrant for search and seizure. The judge may not refuse issuance if probable cause is established. The warrant must specify items to be seized and executed within fourteen days. Failure to comply with the warrant constitutes additional contempt.

Before accepting a plea to violation of an extreme risk protection order, the court shall advise the defendant that such plea may extend the duration of the order. The court must ensure the defendant understands this consequence and enters the plea knowingly and voluntarily. Failure to provide this warning requires vacating the plea upon motion within 21 days after entry of judgment.

On motion or sua sponte, the court may release a defendant held for contempt pending hearing. Release shall be conditioned upon compliance with underlying protective orders. The court may impose additional conditions reasonably necessary to ensure appearance and protect public safety. Failure to comply with release conditions constitutes grounds for immediate detention and adverse inference regarding contempt liability.

A party may appeal an order extending an extreme risk protection order only by leave of court. The motion for leave must be filed within twenty-one days after entry of the order. The moving party shall serve a copy on all parties to the proceeding. The court shall grant or deny leave within fourteen days after filing.

In an extreme risk protection order case, a party aggrieved by a finding of criminal contempt or sentence imposed after a contested violation hearing may appeal as of right. No leave to appeal is required. The notice of appeal must be filed within fourteen days after entry of the order imposing the sentence or finding of contempt.

If service cannot be effected after diligent inquiry, the court may order notice by publication or other means. Upon motion showing that reasonable efforts to locate the party failed, the court shall prescribe the manner of notice, which must be given at least ten days before the hearing date. Such alternative notice constitutes sufficient service for all purposes in this proceeding.

Upon filing a motion for rehearing, the moving party shall serve a copy on all other parties. Any opposing party may file a response within fourteen days after service of the motion. The movant may file a reply within seven days after service of the response. The court may shorten or extend these time periods for good cause shown. Failure to respond does not constitute consent to the motion.

Before entering a final order of adoption, the court shall determine that all appeals regarding termination of parental rights have been resolved or are no longer pending. If an appeal is pending, the court may stay proceedings until final disposition. The petitioner must file proof of such resolution with the clerk within ten days prior to the hearing on finalization.

Upon a finding of indigency in a termination of parental rights appeal, the court shall order the preparation of necessary transcripts at public expense. The clerk must transmit the transcript to the appellate court within thirty days after the order is entered. This provision applies only when the parent files a timely motion for leave to proceed without cost and demonstrates an inability to pay transcription fees.

In neglect proceedings, the Michigan Rules of Evidence do not apply. However, privileges recognized under those rules remain applicable. A party asserting a privilege must object specifically to preserve it. The court shall determine the validity of any claimed privilege and may exclude evidence if the privilege is established.

In these rules, “the Act” refers to the Juvenile Code, MCL 712A.1 through 712A.26. References to specific sections are citations to those statutory provisions unless otherwise indicated. Courts and parties shall interpret such shorthand as designating the governing public act and its corresponding sections within Chapter 712 of the Michigan Compiled Laws.

In family division juvenile proceedings, an individual who has attained eighteen years of age shall no longer be considered a minor for purposes of this rule. Jurisdiction over such individuals terminates upon their eighteenth birthday, unless the court orders otherwise on motion and for good cause shown within thirty days of the attainment of majority.

The prosecutor for the county in which the child resides shall perform duties assigned to the prosecutor under this subchapter.
