These duties may be performed by a staff attorney authorized by the prosecutor. Unless otherwise ordered, filings and notices must be directed to the prosecutor’s office in that county.

A residential treatment facility shall qualify for foster child placement only upon certification by the Department of Health and Human Services. Such certification must confirm compliance with state licensing standards and safety regulations. The court shall not approve a placement order unless the department submits written verification of such qualification within ten days prior to the hearing date.

A facility designated for the secure confinement of adjudicated delinquents shall not be considered a qualified residential treatment program. Such facilities are excluded from the definition regardless of therapeutic services provided. Placement in a secure juvenile detention center does not satisfy the requirement for placement in a qualified residential treatment program under this rule.

A case involving first-degree home invasion is a designated felony. The prosecutor shall file a designation notice within ten days of arraignment. The court may vacate the designation if the offense does not meet statutory criteria or if extraordinary circumstances justify exclusion. Failure to timely designate waives the right to expedited trial scheduling.

Upon transfer from detention, shackles shall be removed unless the court finds they are necessary for security. Before ordering continued restraint, the court must afford counsel an opportunity to be heard. The determination shall be made immediately upon arrival or prior to any proceeding involving the juvenile, whichever occurs first.

The probation officer shall file the assessment report and supervision recommendation with the court clerk within seven days after completion. A copy must be served upon all parties simultaneously. Failure to file the document with the clerk renders the report inadmissible for disposition proceedings, regardless of prior distribution to counsel or other interested parties.

Upon request by the department during pending proceedings, the prosecutor shall provide legal advice regarding the case. Such advice must be rendered within five days of the written request. The prosecutor may decline to advise if the request conflicts with statutory duties or existing court orders. Failure to respond constitutes waiver of objection to departmental actions taken in reliance on prior guidance.

A substitute guardian ad litem may appear only if qualified by the court. Before appearance, the substitute shall file a certification of qualification and disclosure of conflicts. The court shall inquire regarding the substitute’s qualifications and potential conflicts before permitting participation in proceedings involving the child’s best interests. Failure to comply mandates adjournment or appointment of new counsel.

Upon appointment, a guardian ad litem shall file an appearance within ten days. The appearance must disclose any familial, professional, or other relationship with the child, parents, or parties that may affect impartiality. Failure to file timely disclosure constitutes grounds for removal. The court may extend time for good cause shown.

On motion by any party, the court may order genetic testing of the alleged father named in the denial. If testing excludes the denying man and includes the second man, the court shall find the second man to be the legal father. This finding is subject to rebuttal by clear and convincing evidence. The moving party must file such motion within thirty days after service of the denial.

In child protection proceedings, the agency and law enforcement shall disclose all written statements, reports, and notes of oral remarks made by the respondent within fourteen days after filing a petition. Disclosure is mandatory without motion or request. Failure to disclose may result in sanctions. The court may extend time for good cause shown.

In child protection proceedings, a party producing records containing confidential information shall redact such information prior to disclosure. The party must serve notice of the redaction on all other parties within three days after production. On motion by any party, the court may order inspection of the redacted portions to determine if further disclosure is required in the interest of justice or child safety.

The prosecutor shall disclose to the defense all documents in the prosecutor’s possession or control that are material to the detention hearing, including intake scoring instruments and psychological evaluations ordered by the court. Disclosure must occur at least three days before the hearing date, unless good cause is shown for a shorter period. Failure to disclose may result in exclusion of the evidence.

On motion of a party, the court shall order disclosure of underlying documents supporting a probation or disposition recommendation. Disclosure must occur within seven days before the hearing date. The court may deny discovery if it finds good cause, such as undue burden or irreparable harm to the juvenile’s interests.

On motion filed at least ten days before trial, a party seeking to exclude spectators from the courtroom gallery during a child witness’s testimony shall serve written notice on all parties. The notice must specify the requested accommodation and the reasons therefor. The court may grant relief if necessary to protect the witness’s well-being or ensure reliable testimony, subject to the defendant’s constitutional rights.

On motion or sua sponte, the court shall notify any other Michigan court having jurisdiction over the child within ten days of filing. The family division may proceed only if the other court consents in writing or fails to object within twenty days. If concurrent jurisdiction exists, the courts shall coordinate proceedings to avoid conflicting orders.

In child protective proceedings, a party may file documents by facsimile transmission if the court has authorized such filing. The transmitting party must ensure the document is legible and includes all required signatures. Upon receipt, the clerk shall stamp the document with the date and time of receipt. A party filing by facsimile must serve a copy on all other parties within one day after filing.

A party intending to offer photographic evidence at trial shall file copies with the clerk within seven days before the proceeding. Upon admission, such photographs become part of the official case record. The court may order earlier filing or restrict access to protect privacy interests. Failure to comply constitutes a waiver of the right to introduce the evidence unless good cause is shown.

A delinquency proceeding against a minor shall commence by filing a verified petition. The petition must be captioned in accordance with court rules, signed by the prosecuting attorney, and verified under oath. It shall state the facts constituting the alleged offense and specify the time and place of the occurrence. Failure to verify or properly caption the petition does not invalidate the proceeding if cured within ten days after objection.

In a delinquency petition, the respondent shall be named as the minor child. If a guardian has been appointed for the minor, the guardian shall be served with process in addition to the parents. Failure to serve the guardian does not invalidate proceedings if service upon the parents is completed within the time prescribed by law. The court may order additional parties joined on motion showing necessity.

On motion of the prosecutor for good cause shown, the court may adjourn a preliminary examination in a juvenile case involving a serious offense listed under statute. Such adjournment shall not exceed thirty days from the scheduled date. No further continuances are permitted absent extraordinary circumstances demonstrated to the satisfaction of the court.

Upon motion or sua sponte, the court may consider the juvenile’s prior record of violent conduct when determining whether detention is necessary to ensure appearance or protect public safety. This consideration shall not prejudice the determination of guilt at trial. The court must state findings on the record supporting any decision to detain based on prior history.

Upon motion or sua sponte, the court may release a juvenile to a parent’s custody pending trial if the judge finds reasonable assurance of appearance. The court shall impose conditions necessary to ensure attendance and protect public safety, including electronic monitoring or curfew restrictions, upon a showing that unconditional release poses an unacceptable risk of non-appearance.

Upon release of a juvenile at a preliminary hearing, the court may impose conditions necessary to ensure appearance and protect public safety. Such conditions shall include mandatory school attendance and satisfactory conduct. Failure to comply with these educational requirements constitutes a violation of release terms, subjecting the juvenile to immediate revocation proceedings and potential detention pending further order.

Upon dismissal of a petition or finding that no offense was committed, the court shall order immediate destruction of all fingerprints, photographs, and arrest records taken in connection with the juvenile’s detention. The clerk shall transmit this order to the law enforcement agency that made the arrest, which must destroy the records within 30 days and certify compliance to the court.

Upon transfer from district court following preliminary examination, the case shall be treated as commenced in the family division. Within fourteen days after transfer, the prosecutor must file with the court a copy of the information or complaint and all exhibits admitted at the preliminary examination. Failure to file these documents within the prescribed time may result in dismissal of the charges without prejudice.

On motion or sua sponte, the court may transfer jurisdiction to circuit court if the juvenile violates probation after a prior disposition. Such transfer constitutes a change in venue rather than an incremental sanction within the dispositional ladder. The court shall hold a hearing before ordering transfer, ensuring the juvenile’s right to counsel is preserved during proceedings determining adult jurisdiction.

At the best-interests stage of a waiver hearing, the court may consider hearsay reports and other evidence not admissible under ordinary evidentiary rules. Such evidence is admissible if it possesses sufficient indicia of reliability. The court shall weigh all relevant factors, including the nature of the offense and the child’s background, to determine whether waiver serves the best interests of justice and public safety.

Upon denial of transfer to adult court, the juvenile shall be released from detention within forty-eight hours unless the court finds probable cause for continued detention based on flight risk or danger to the community. If detained, trial must commence within thirty days. No monetary bail shall be imposed as a condition of release in juvenile proceedings.

Upon setting a designation hearing, the court shall enter the date on the record. Unless all parties are personally present and waive notice, the clerk must serve written notice of the hearing date to each party within three days. Service may be accomplished by mail or electronic transmission. Failure to provide timely notice does not invalidate the hearing if no prejudice is shown.

Upon motion for transfer to adult court, the court shall consider whether the juvenile is an enrolled member of a federally recognized Indian tribe. This factor must be weighed in determining if transfer serves the interests of justice and public safety. The court shall make specific findings regarding tribal status on the record before ordering any transfer.

Upon binding over, the court shall order detention in an adult facility if the juvenile is charged with a felony. No additional consent is required. The court must determine that confinement serves public safety or ensures appearance. Detention orders remain effective until trial conclusion or discharge, subject to periodic review every thirty days.

In a designated case, a juvenile defendant may waive the right to trial by jury only after consultation with counsel. The court shall not accept such a waiver unless the record affirmatively shows that the juvenile has been advised of the nature of the charge and the consequences of waiving the jury right by legal counsel. Any waiver obtained prior to such consultation is void.

On motion of the prosecuting attorney, the burden is upon the People to prove by clear and convincing evidence that the juvenile should be sentenced as an adult. Before deciding, the court shall consider the nature of the offense, the juvenile’s history, and the best interests of society. The court may order a psychological or psychiatric examination.

The court shall provide written notice to the juvenile at least ten days before the review hearing. The notice must warn that the judge may impose a sentence if conditions are violated and advise the juvenile of the right to counsel. If the juvenile is not represented, the notice shall state that counsel will be appointed upon request.

Before imposing an adult sentence, the court must find that public safety requires such disposition. In making this determination, the court shall weigh the defendant’s conduct during the period of abeyance against the need to protect the public from criminal conduct by the juvenile.

Upon conviction of a new felony while on probation for a delayed sentence, the court shall revoke probation and impose the suspended sentence. The court may not extend probation or modify the original disposition without vacating the prior order. Sentencing shall occur within ninety days of the new conviction, subject to applicable statutory maximums and mandatory minimum penalties established by law.

Before filing a petition in a protective proceeding, the court must conduct a preliminary inquiry. Upon finding probable cause that the respondent is incapacitated or vulnerable, the judge shall order the petition filed. The court may appoint counsel for the respondent during the inquiry. Failure to establish probable cause requires dismissal of the matter without prejudice.

Upon taking a child into protective custody, the officer shall file a written statement with the court within twenty-four hours. The statement must specify the facts and circumstances constituting probable cause for the removal, including immediate threats to the child’s health or safety. Failure to file such statement within the prescribed time renders the detention unlawful unless good cause is shown.

At the initial hearing, the court shall inquire whether any party or child is an enrolled member of a federally recognized tribe. If the response indicates potential tribal jurisdiction, the court must immediately notify the tribe and stay proceedings pending determination of exclusive state jurisdiction under the Indian Child Welfare Act.

If the court finds no reasonable cause to believe the child is an abused or neglected child, it shall dismiss the petition. Upon dismissal, the court shall order the immediate return of the child to the parent or legal custodian, unless the child is in foster care and a separate permanency plan requires continued placement. The court may refer the family to social services.

The court shall not place a child in foster care at a preliminary hearing unless it finds clear and convincing evidence that leaving the child with a parent poses an immediate danger to the child’s physical health, safety, or moral welfare. This finding must be made on the record before any order for temporary custody is issued.

Before ordering placement in foster care, the court shall find by clear and convincing evidence that the proposed setting is safe, suitable, and appropriate for the child’s needs. The court must consider the least restrictive environment necessary to protect the child while preserving family ties whenever possible.

On motion of the department, the court may excuse reunification services if clear and convincing evidence establishes that a parent was convicted of felony child abuse or neglect, or aiding in a homicide involving a sibling. The motion must be filed within thirty days of the conviction becoming final. The court shall hold a hearing to determine whether statutory exceptions apply before terminating efforts.

Upon placement of a child with a relative or non-relative caregiver during preliminary proceedings, the court shall order an evaluation of the household. The evaluating agency must submit its written report to the court within fourteen days of the order. The judge shall review the report and determine the appropriateness of the placement before any further custody orders are issued, ensuring the child’s safety and well-being remain paramount throughout the process.

Upon removal of a child from guardianship at a preliminary hearing, the court shall immediately determine the guardian’s visitation rights if the guardian demonstrates ongoing contact. The court may issue temporary orders regarding such contact pending final disposition, provided the best interests of the child are served and no undue delay occurs in establishing parental custody arrangements.

If the court orders removal at the preliminary hearing, the agency shall file a written case plan within thirty days. The plan must include services designed to reunify the family or achieve permanency. The court may extend this period for good cause shown, but no extension shall exceed an additional thirty days without further judicial approval.

On motion by any party after disposition, the court shall hold a review hearing if it determines that the child’s current placement is not in the best interests of the child. In deciding whether to modify the placement, the court must weigh the stability of the home, the child’s adjustment, and the likelihood of reunification or permanent placement, ensuring the order serves the child’s welfare.

In neglect proceedings where children remain with parents, the court shall schedule an initial review hearing within sixty days of petition authorization. Subsequent reviews shall occur at intervals not exceeding ninety days during the first twelve months. After twelve months, the court may extend intervals to one hundred eighty days if necessary for case management, provided such extensions do not compromise child safety or statutory deadlines.

Upon an emergency removal of a child previously adjudicated, the court shall reduce its findings to writing within twenty-four hours. The written order must state the reasons for continued custody or detention. Before entry of the order, the court shall afford each party an opportunity to be heard and to present evidence regarding the necessity of the emergency action.

If no relative or fit person is willing to serve as guardian, the court shall order placement in foster care unless clear and convincing evidence establishes that another permanency plan serves the child’s best interests. The court must state specific findings on the record justifying any deviation from foster care placement.

The court shall not consider a motion to terminate parental rights filed prior to the scheduled permanency hearing unless the agency demonstrates substantial new evidence of unfitness or that termination serves the child’s best interests. Absent such showing, the court must defer consideration until the next review hearing mandated by statute.

The court shall conduct a review hearing within ninety days of termination and every six months thereafter during the first year if the child remains in foster care. If the permanent plan is placement with a relative, no further review hearings are required unless the court orders otherwise on motion or sua sponte to ensure the child’s safety and well-being.

Upon receipt of notice that guardianship assistance has terminated, the court shall terminate the guardianship without further motion or hearing. A party seeking to continue the guardianship must file a motion within fourteen days after receiving notice. The court may hold a hearing only if a timely motion is filed.

On motion by any party or sua sponte, the court may modify or terminate guardianship if clear and convincing evidence demonstrates it is no longer in the child’s best interests. A moving party shall file a petition specifying grounds for relief within thirty days of discovering facts warranting termination. The court shall hold an evidentiary hearing before entering an order altering custody rights.

On motion of the prosecuting attorney or law enforcement officer, the court shall initiate contempt proceedings for violation of a protection order issued to a minor. No filing fee shall be charged for such motions. The motion must be filed within thirty days of the alleged violation.

Upon detention of a juvenile for alleged violation of a protection order, if the officer cannot secure a parent’s promise to appear, the officer shall immediately transport the juvenile to a designated facility. Detention without such transport is prohibited unless authorized by judicial warrant or exigent circumstances requiring immediate custody for safety.

Upon filing a request for review of a referee’s recommended disposition, the court shall schedule a hearing within fourteen days. The court may extend this period only upon finding good cause. A party is not entitled to a specific courtroom date absent such scheduling order. The judge must rule on the merits promptly after the hearing concludes.

A party may seek leave to appeal a child protective order not otherwise immediately appealable by filing a motion with the Court of Appeals within twenty-one days after entry of the order. The motion shall state the grounds for relief and attach a copy of the order. The court shall grant or deny leave to appeal within thirty days after filing.

In child protective proceedings where appeal is as of right, the court shall appoint counsel using the specific form designated for such cases. A generic appointment order is insufficient. Counsel must be appointed within ten days after filing notice of appeal or entry of the appealable order, whichever occurs later, if requested by a party entitled to representation.

On motion filed within 21 days after entry of judgment or order, the court may extend the time for filing any required document if failure to act was caused by excusable neglect. No extension shall exceed 6 months from the original deadline unless the court finds extraordinary circumstances warranting relief. The moving party must demonstrate good cause and serve all parties.

On motion of any party, the court may transfer an action to the circuit court if it appears that relief sought is beyond the district court’s jurisdiction or authority. The motion must be filed within 21 days after discovery of facts supporting transfer. The receiving court shall determine whether transfer is appropriate in the interest of justice and judicial economy.

In civil infraction proceedings, the citation issued by an officer serves as the complaint. No separate complaint need be filed. Upon issuance of the citation, the case is commenced. The defendant shall file a response within twenty-one days after service of the citation. Failure to respond constitutes a default.

In any forcible entry and detainer action, the complaint or summons served upon the defendant must contain a conspicuous notice informing the defendant of the right to retain legal counsel to assist in preparing a response and asserting available defenses. Failure to include this statutory notice shall not invalidate the service but may constitute grounds for relief from judgment if prejudice is demonstrated.

A party appearing without written pleadings may respond orally to allegations. The court shall record such oral responses verbatim in the minutes or transcript. Failure to request contemporaneous transcription or entry into the record constitutes a waiver of the right to appeal based on those specific factual admissions. Oral responses are binding unless corrected by the court before judgment.

If a counterclaim exceeds the district court’s jurisdictional monetary limit, the court shall transfer the entire action to the circuit court. This transfer includes all claims, defenses, and counterclaims arising from the same transaction or occurrence. The parties must file any pending motions with the circuit court within ten days of the order of transfer.

If a tenant files an affidavit stating that assistance has been applied for, the landlord must file written proof of nonpayment within ten days after service of the summons. If the landlord fails to file such proof within the prescribed time, the court shall dismiss the complaint without prejudice. The court may extend this period for good cause shown.

The stay of eviction proceedings pending determination of rental assistance shall expire automatically ninety days after the date of entry of the order granting the stay, unless extended by the court for good cause shown on motion filed before expiration. Upon expiration, the case shall be restored to the active calendar for further proceedings.

The judgment in a possession action must state the tenant’s right to vacate or pay rent due within fourteen days after entry of judgment. Failure to comply within this period constitutes a waiver of such rights, subjecting the tenant to immediate execution of the writ. The court shall include this notice on the face of the judgment order.

Upon entry of judgment in small claims proceedings, the ordinary rules of civil procedure govern all post-judgment matters, including enforcement, appeals, and motions to vacate. The small claims statute ceases to apply except as expressly provided herein. Parties must comply with standard procedural timelines and requirements for any further relief sought from the court.

A plaintiff may waive jurisdictional excess to maintain small claims status. Judgment shall not exceed the statutory limit. A party seeking recovery of amounts exceeding that limit must file a separate action in a court of competent jurisdiction within thirty days after entry of judgment. The separate action is barred if the initial claim was dismissed for failure to prosecute.

On motion of a party demonstrating insufficient notice, the court shall reschedule the hearing. If the defendant failed to appear due to inadequate service, no additional filing fee is required. The moving party must file the motion within ten days after the scheduled hearing date. The court may impose conditions necessary to ensure proper notice for the rescheduled proceeding.

If both parties appear in person, remote participation is prohibited. The court may continue the trial only upon finding good cause shown by either party or on its own motion. A continuance shall not be granted solely for convenience. Any request for continuation must be made before the trial commences.

Unless this chapter provides otherwise, the general civil rules govern proceedings in probate matters. Where a specific procedure is not prescribed herein, parties shall comply with applicable civil procedural standards regarding pleadings, discovery, and motions. The court may adapt civil rules to fit the unique nature of probate administration, ensuring consistency while respecting statutory mandates exclusive to this chapter.

A personal representative must commence an action by complaint rather than petition when the matter involves a claim against a third party not arising from administration. The caption shall identify the estate as plaintiff and name all defendants. The complaint must be filed with the probate court clerk and served upon each defendant within twenty-one days after filing, unless otherwise ordered by the court for good cause shown.

In probate proceedings, service of process upon a resident of a state hospital shall be effected by delivering a copy to the superintendent or authorized agent of the facility. Personal service by a private process server is prohibited without prior court order. The recipient must acknowledge receipt within three days. Failure to comply renders service void.

On motion showing diligent inquiry failed to locate an heir, the court may order notice by publication. The moving party shall file proof of publication within ten days after final insertion. Once ordered, publication is sufficient for all subsequent proceedings in the matter unless the court orders otherwise or actual service becomes feasible.

If an interested person cannot be reached after diligent inquiry, any party may move ex parte for an order prescribing notice by publication or other means. The court shall grant the motion if satisfied that reasonable efforts to locate the person failed. The order must specify the method and duration of notice.

The fiduciary shall serve the initial inventory of assets upon the protected person within thirty days after filing. This service requirement applies regardless of any prior order permitting substituted service for annual accountings. Failure to serve the inventory personally or by certified mail constitutes a waiver of the stand-in arrangement for that specific document.

Upon entry of an order approving an annual account, the register shall serve a copy of the order on all interested persons within fourteen days. Service is complete upon mailing. If the register fails to serve, any interested person may move the court for an order compelling service or awarding costs.

A party must hand-deliver a probate petition to all interested parties at least seven days before the hearing date. If a statute prescribes a different period for service, that statutory period controls. The court may shorten these time limits on motion for good cause shown. Failure to comply with the required service period constitutes grounds for continuance of the hearing.

A party may file a petition to raise new matters in an open estate. The petitioner shall serve a copy of the petition on all interested persons within fourteen days after filing. Service must be made by first-class mail or personal delivery. The court may grant relief upon good cause shown, provided that the rights of other interested persons are not prejudiced by the delay.

If the court finds probable cause that the settlor lacks capacity, it shall order notice to the settlor’s legal representative or conservator. Such representative is an interested party entitled to participate in proceedings. Notice must be served within ten days of the finding. Failure to serve notice may result in dismissal of the petition or stay of proceedings pending appointment of a guardian.

In an action to settle a trustee’s account for a revocable trust, the trustee shall serve notice of the hearing on the settlor if alive. Notice need not be served on contingent remaindermen or beneficiaries whose interests are subject to divestment upon the settlor’s death, unless the court orders otherwise on motion showing good cause for such service.

The petitioner shall serve notice of the petition upon all persons named in the statute and any other person whose interest may be affected by the order. Service must occur at least twenty-one days before the hearing date. The court may, on motion or sua sponte, require additional notice to protect interested parties not otherwise listed.

Upon filing a demand for notice, the clerk must promptly notify all parties of record. Thereafter, every party or attorney of record shall serve copies of all subsequent pleadings, motions, and orders on the person who filed the demand within three days after service upon other parties. Failure to comply constitutes a waiver of right to object to lack of service.

Upon transfer of venue for convenience, the transferring court shall transmit the complete case file to the receiving court. Within ten days after entry of the order of transfer, the clerk shall certify and forward all pleadings, exhibits, and records. No additional documents are required unless specifically ordered by the transferring judge. The receiving court shall maintain jurisdiction upon receipt of the certified file.

In contested guardianship proceedings, automatic exchange of information under civil rules is suspended. A party may serve discovery requests on an interested person who is not a formal party only upon leave of court granted for good cause shown. Such service shall comply with probate procedural requirements and must occur within thirty days after the order granting leave.

On motion of a ward or guardian ad litem, the court shall hold guardianship proceedings in person if the ward requests physical presence, provided such request is made within ten days before the hearing date. This right applies to wards of any age. The court may deny the motion only upon finding that in-person attendance poses a substantial risk to the ward’s health or safety.

In contested probate proceedings, the court may hold scheduling conferences and enter a scheduling order governing discovery and pretrial matters. Such orders shall be entered within 60 days after the first responsive pleading or upon motion by any party. The court may modify the schedule for good cause shown. These procedures apply unless inconsistent with specific provisions of this rule.

On motion of any interested person, the court may reopen an administratively closed estate to administer newly discovered assets. The former personal representative shall not automatically resume duties. The court shall appoint a successor personal representative or order specific administration as justice requires, subject to notice and hearing.

In any probate proceeding involving mental health matters, a party demanding a jury trial shall file a written demand within fourteen days after service of the initial pleading raising such issues. The court shall conduct the trial in accordance with ordinary civil jury procedures unless specific statutory provisions governing mental health commitments expressly provide otherwise. Failure to timely demand a jury constitutes a waiver of the right to a jury trial.

A personal representative moving residence outside the state must file notice of the new address with the court clerk within ten days of the move. The representative shall serve a copy on all interested persons. Electronic filing satisfies the filing requirement but does not excuse service obligations. Failure to provide timely notice may result in sanctions or removal from office upon motion by any interested party.

On motion of any interested person or sua sponte, the court may order the closing of an estate that has remained open without action for more than one year. The court shall assess reasonable attorney fees and costs against the personal representative’s counsel if the delay resulted from counsel’s neglect. Such assessment is mandatory unless the court finds good cause exists to excuse the failure to proceed.

These rules do not apply to small estate assignments under MCL 700.3981. A person seeking assignment of a decedent’s small estate shall file an affidavit with the circuit court clerk. The court shall not exercise jurisdiction over such proceedings. Parties must comply with statutory requirements for small estates exclusively.

The personal representative shall file an inventory listing all assets. For each bank or credit union holding estate funds, the inventory must specify the exact branch location where accounts are maintained. General corporate headquarters addresses are insufficient unless the account is held solely at the main office. The court may require additional specificity on motion to ensure accurate asset identification and creditor notification.

In a supervised estate, the personal representative may file a summary account without itemizing each receipt and payment if the court grants leave. The filing must state that heirs may object within thirty days of service. Failure to object constitutes waiver of rights regarding the summarized items, unless fraud or mistake is shown.

Within thirty days after retention, an attorney representing a personal representative shall serve written notice of the proposed fee arrangement upon all known heirs and devisees. The notice must specify the basis for compensation and estimated costs. If any heir objects to the fees within twenty days, the court may require further proceedings to determine reasonableness before approval.

On motion by a party objecting to transfer based on alleged tribal court incapacity, the court shall hold an evidentiary hearing within fourteen days. The moving party bears the burden of proving the tribal court lacks jurisdiction or procedural capacity. Absent clear and convincing evidence of such deficiency, the court must order removal to tribal jurisdiction pursuant to federal law.

Upon motion or sua sponte determination that a minor may be a member of an Indian tribe, the court shall order an investigation into tribal membership status within ten days. The clerk shall mail a copy of the order to the Department of Health and Human Services, the child’s guardian, and all parties of record.

The court may rely upon a written evaluation submitted by an examining clinician without requiring that person to testify. Such evaluation shall be filed with the clerk at least fourteen days before the hearing date, unless good cause is shown for a shorter period. A party may object to the admission of the evaluation on motion filed within seven days after service of the report.

Upon petition to modify guardianship, if the ward objects, the court shall appoint separate counsel for the ward within seven days. The previously appointed guardian ad litem shall continue serving unless the court orders otherwise. The new counsel must file an initial appearance within five days of appointment.

Within thirty days after the close of each accounting period, the conservator shall file an account with the clerk and serve a copy on all interested persons. The copy served must include the final inventory, if not previously filed, and a statement of receipts and disbursements. Failure to file or serve within the prescribed time may result in sanctions or removal upon motion by any interested person.

Upon appointment of a trustee under a will, the court shall issue letters testamentary or an order confirming authority. If no letters issue, the register shall provide a certified copy of the order appointing the trustee. This document serves as prima facie evidence of authority to third parties. The trustee must present this certification within thirty days of appointment to establish standing for asset administration.

Upon entering an order placing a trust under court supervision, the court shall specify the scope of that supervision. The order must detail the specific powers retained by the trustee and those requiring prior judicial approval. A generic designation of supervision without particularized terms is insufficient. The court may modify these terms on motion or sua sponte to ensure adequate oversight.

In mental health commitment proceedings, an individual seeking to proceed without counsel must make such election in writing. Before accepting the waiver, the court shall conduct a hearing to determine if the election is made knowingly, intelligently, and voluntarily. If the court finds the waiver valid, it shall appoint standby counsel to assist the individual throughout the proceeding.

The court shall ensure that any commitment hearing conducted at a hospital unit is held in a setting that preserves the dignity of the proceedings and protects the privacy of the respondent. The location must provide adequate security, reasonable accommodations for participants, and conditions substantially equivalent to those available in a courtroom, ensuring that the rights of all parties are fully safeguarded during the hearing.

The respondent may demand a jury trial by filing a written demand within ten days after service of the petition. Failure to file such demand constitutes a waiver of the right to a jury trial. The petitioning hospital shall not be entitled to demand a jury trial in any civil commitment proceeding. The court shall determine all factual issues without a jury unless a valid demand is timely filed by the respondent.

The party filing the treatment report shall make the author available for cross-examination upon request by opposing counsel. A copy of the report must be served on all parties within seven days prior to the hearing. Failure to produce the author or serve the report constitutes a waiver of reliance on its contents, unless the court grants leave for good cause shown.

Upon readmission following leave exceeding fourteen days, the facility director shall file a notice with the court within ten days. The notice must state the date of return and certify that the patient was informed of their right to counsel and the nature of proceedings. Failure to file timely notice constitutes grounds for dismissal of pending petitions.

Upon return of a resident with a developmental disability after a leave exceeding ten days, the facility administrator shall file notice with the court within five days. The notice must inform the resident that they may challenge the return. A copy shall be served on the resident’s guardian or representative simultaneously. Failure to provide timely notice waives the right to contest the validity of the return unless good cause is shown.

Upon readmission of a committed person from leave, the director shall immediately file a report with the court. Within ten days of filing, the court shall notify the person of the right to contest the readmission and request a hearing. Failure to file within this period renders the readmission voidable upon motion by the person or counsel.

Upon entry of an order in a new guardianship proceeding involving a person under an existing order from another county, the courts shall confer to determine which court retains jurisdiction over the original file. The transferring court must transmit all records within thirty days after such determination, unless the parties agree otherwise or the receiving court orders immediate transfer to prevent prejudice.

The former juvenile rules within the probate chapter are repealed and superseded by these rules. All proceedings involving juveniles shall be governed exclusively by the current Juvenile Rules. Citations to prior rule numbers are deemed references to their substantive successors herein. Parties must comply with the renumbered provisions effective immediately upon adoption.

Notwithstanding juvenile status, general criminal procedure rules apply to prosecutions by complaint in district court until transfer or dismissal. The prosecutor must file charges within statutory limits. The defendant is entitled to speedy trial rights and discovery under general provisions unless specifically excluded by juvenile subchapter mandates. District courts retain jurisdiction for preliminary proceedings consistent with general criminal standards.

These rules shall be construed to secure just, speedy, and inexpensive determination of every criminal proceeding. The court must administer these rules to eliminate unnecessary delay, expense, and technicality. In interpreting any provision, the court shall favor construction that promotes simplicity in procedure, fairness in administration, and the elimination of unjustifiable expense and delay.

A defendant appearing via video conferencing technology may request to appear in person. If the court grants such a request, all parties and the presiding judge must appear in person at the hearing. The court shall not compel any party or judicial officer to participate remotely if one participant insists on physical presence, unless all participants expressly consent to hybrid proceedings.

The court may set release conditions on the face of an arrest warrant. Such conditions shall specify the amount and type of security required for pre-arraignment release. The court may condition this release upon the defendant’s appearance within a specified period following arrest. Failure to appear within that period voids the release authority, requiring immediate custody pending judicial review.

Upon failure of a defendant to appear at a scheduled proceeding, the court shall not issue a bench warrant until seven days have elapsed from the date of the scheduled appearance. This waiting period excludes Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays. The court may shorten this period upon a showing of good cause or immediate danger to public safety.

A defendant with an outstanding bench warrant may voluntarily surrender to the issuing court at any time, regardless of the warrant’s age. No outer time limit applies to such voluntary surrender. Upon appearance, the court shall set conditions for release or detention consistent with applicable law. This right is not waived by the passage of time since the warrant’s issuance.

The court may impose any condition reasonably necessary to assure appearance at trial or protect public safety. If no specific statutory condition applies, the court shall order release subject to such other conditions as are just and proper under the circumstances. The defendant must comply with all imposed conditions. Failure to comply constitutes grounds for revocation of release.

If the court denies the ten percent deposit option, any surety bond filed to secure release must be in the full amount of the bail set by the court. A bondsman shall not issue a bond for less than the total sum unless the court expressly orders a reduction. The bond remains effective until discharged or forfeited according to law.

The court may consider community supervision offers in setting bond conditions. A party seeking credit for such offers shall file a written motion specifying the supervisors’ identities and contact information within three days of arraignment. The court shall evaluate the reliability of proposed supervisors before imposing conditions. Failure to provide verifiable supervisor details within the prescribed time waives consideration of community supervision as a mitigating factor in bond determination.

Upon arraignment on an information in circuit court, the judge shall determine conditions of release independently. The prior bond set in district court is not binding. The circuit court may modify or revoke release conditions without a showing of changed circumstances, provided the defendant receives notice and an opportunity to be heard regarding the proposed terms.

On motion to modify conditions of release, the moving party shall bear the initial burden of proof. The court may order the parties to present evidence in a different sequence if justice requires. Unless otherwise ordered, the movant must establish by clear and convincing evidence that changed circumstances warrant modification before the opposing party responds.

Upon dismissal of charges or acquittal, the court shall refund the full deposit amount to the defendant within fourteen days. No portion of the deposit shall be retained by the court for administrative costs unless specifically authorized by statute. The refund must be issued without interest.

On motion of a defendant, the court shall schedule separate probable cause conferences for each codefendant unless the court finds that joint proceedings are necessary to prevent inconsistent findings or undue delay. The conference must occur within fourteen days after arraignment. A party seeking separation must file the motion promptly upon learning of the co-defendant’s status.

Upon filing of a felony complaint charging multiple defendants, the court shall schedule separate preliminary examinations for each defendant unless all defendants consent to a joint proceeding. The prosecutor may move to sever the examinations at any time before commencement. The court must grant such motion if joinder would prejudice a defendant’s rights or impede a fair trial.

Upon acceptance of a guilty plea in district court for a felony offense, the judge shall immediately transfer the case to circuit court. The circuit judge shall impose sentence. If no circuit judge is available, the district judge may accept the plea and set a date for sentencing before a circuit judge within thirty days.

A party must file a witness list with the charging document. The list shall identify all witnesses known to the investigating officers at the time of filing. A party may amend the list on motion for good cause shown, within ten days after notice of intent to call additional witnesses. Failure to include a witness precludes testimony unless the court finds prejudice would result.

Before accepting a plea to an information, the court shall advise the defendant of rights and consequences. The prosecutor need not read the charge aloud if the defendant waives such reading in writing or on the record. The court must ensure the waiver is knowing and voluntary before proceeding with the plea colloquy.

On motion of a party or sua sponte, the court may order separate trials if joinder appears to prejudice a defendant or confuse the issues. The court shall consider whether offenses arise from a common scheme or plan. If joined, the court must ensure fair determination of each charge’s merits. Prejudice outweighs efficiency only upon clear showing.

On motion by a defendant, the court shall order separate trials if joinder prejudices a party. In ruling, the court must weigh the risk of cumulative evidence against judicial economy. If the proofs against one defendant are minimal and distinct from others, separation may be granted to prevent unfair prejudice, provided no mutually exclusive defenses exist. The court shall specify conditions for severance within five days of the motion.

On motion by a party seeking interlocutory review of an order excluding evidence, the trial court shall stay further proceedings pending disposition of the appeal only if good cause is shown. Absent such showing, the court shall proceed with the trial without delay. The moving party must file the motion within ten days after entry of the challenged order.

If the court declines to accept a plea agreement immediately, it shall advise the defendant on the record that the court may reject the agreement later, that the defendant is not bound by the agreement if rejected, and that the defendant may withdraw the plea before the court rules. The court shall afford the defendant an opportunity to object or withdraw the plea prior to final disposition.

Before accepting a plea of guilty but mentally ill, the court shall determine that the defendant suffers from a mental disease or defect that substantially impairs his capacity to appreciate the criminality of his conduct or conform his conduct to the requirements of law. This determination must be made on the record after hearing evidence and argument, independent of the standard plea colloquy requirements.

Before accepting a plea of insanity, the court shall advise the defendant that a verdict of not guilty by reason of insanity may result in commitment to a mental health facility for treatment until restored to competency or cleared for release. The court shall determine that the defendant understands these consequences and voluntarily enters the plea.

If the court finds the plea colloquy defective, it shall vacate the plea and sentence. The defendant may then plead not guilty or withdraw the plea. The court shall set a new trial date or schedule further proceedings as appropriate. This relief is mandatory upon such finding and does not require additional justification by the moving party.

The court shall select twelve jurors for deliberation by lot or other method. If an alternate replaces a juror after deliberations commence, the jury must resume deliberations with the new member. The court shall instruct the jury to disregard prior discussions and begin anew. This substitution requires a finding of good cause and ensures impartiality.

The court shall not direct a party to call specific witnesses or introduce particular evidence. The order of proof and selection of witnesses remain within the discretion of each party, subject only to the court’s authority to control proceedings for efficiency and fairness. No party may be compelled by judicial directive to present testimony or exhibits that the party elects not to offer.

Before declaring a mistrial in a criminal case, the court shall afford counsel for each party an opportunity to be heard. The record must reflect any objection or position stated by a party regarding the declaration. Failure to state a position on the record constitutes a waiver of the right to appeal the mistrial declaration based on that specific ground.

After the prosecution rests, a defendant moving for acquittal need not make any statement or reservation of rights to preserve the right to present evidence in defense. Failure to state an intention to offer evidence shall not be deemed a waiver of that right. The court may deny the motion without prejudice to the defendant’s subsequent presentation of testimony or other proof.

Upon receipt of a verdict, the court shall inquire of each juror individually whether they assent to it. If any juror does not assent, the court must discharge the jury without further deliberation. The court may not permit individual questioning regarding the validity of the verdict or the mental processes employed in reaching it.

The investigator shall include in the report all prior juvenile adjudications and adult convictions. Upon request by either party or sua sponte, the court may order disclosure of sealed juvenile records relevant to sentencing. The report must be filed within thirty days after the defendant enters a plea of guilty or no contest, unless good cause for extension is shown.

The court shall hold a hearing on the record to resolve any disputed facts in the presentence investigation report before imposing sentence. A party must file objections within fourteen days of receiving the report. If the court finds an objection meritorious, it shall make specific findings regarding the disputed facts and state its reasons for accepting or rejecting them.

Before imposing sentence, the court shall address the defendant personally to determine if he wishes to make a statement or present any information in mitigation. The court may not impose sentence unless the defendant has been afforded this opportunity. Failure to comply with this requirement constitutes reversible error.

The prosecution bears the burden of proving actual loss by a preponderance of the evidence. A party challenging the presentence report’s restitution figure must file written objections within fourteen days after receipt. The court shall hold an evidentiary hearing upon request, considering only competent evidence submitted by either party to determine the precise amount owed to the victim.

If the prosecutor appeals an order granting post-conviction relief, the court shall appoint counsel for the defendant within seven days of receiving notice of the appeal. The prior appointment does not extend to this separate proceeding. Counsel must file a notice of appearance and defend the relief granted unless the defendant waives representation in writing.

On motion to alter restitution after judgment, the moving party shall serve a copy of the motion and supporting documents on the prosecutor and the victim within seven days after filing. Service on the victim may be made by the moving party or through the prosecutor. Failure to serve the victim as required shall constitute grounds for denying the motion.

On motion filed within fourteen days after verdict or dismissal, a party may request a new trial. The court shall grant relief only upon showing manifest injustice or irregularity. If the court denies the motion, it shall state specific findings of fact and conclusions of law supporting the denial. Failure to file timely waives the right to appeal based on grounds raised in the motion.

Upon imposition of sentence for probation revocation, the court shall advise the defendant that an appeal may be taken as of right from the order of revocation. The advice shall specify that the appeal lies only from the revocation order and not from the underlying conviction or sentence imposed at trial or upon plea.

On motion by the prosecutor or victim, the court shall restore a vacated conviction if restitution remains unpaid. Before restoration, the court must provide written notice to the defendant and afford a reasonable opportunity to be heard. The defendant may contest the amount owed or demonstrate compliance. Restoration is effective upon entry of order unless stayed pending appeal.

A postconviction motion shall not exceed twenty-five pages. Supporting briefs are prohibited unless authorized by the court. The moving party must file the motion with the clerk. The court may schedule a hearing on its own initiative or upon request, but no hearing is required unless the court orders one. Failure to comply with page limits constitutes grounds for dismissal without prejudice.

Upon order of the court requiring the People to respond to a postconviction motion, the People shall file their answer within twenty-one days after service of the order. The length of the answer is not capped by rule but must be concise and responsive. The court may extend the time for good cause shown. Failure to comply may result in sanctions or adverse inference against the non-complying party.

On motion or sua sponte, the court may order parties to submit affidavits, documents, or sworn written answers to specific questions before setting an evidentiary hearing. Parties must comply within 14 days of the order. Failure to respond constitutes a waiver of objections and may result in adverse inference findings against the non-complying party.

The court shall dismiss any postconviction claim previously rejected on direct appeal unless the claim relies on newly discovered evidence or a constitutional right not previously available. A party raising such a claim must file a motion specifying the factual basis within thirty days of filing the petition. Failure to comply mandates dismissal without prejudice to claims not barred by res judicata.

A notice of appeal must be filed within twenty-one days after entry of the order denying post-conviction relief. If a timely motion for reconsideration is filed, the time to appeal runs from the entry of the order disposing of that motion. Filing such a motion does not extend the time for appealing the original judgment or sentence unless the order explicitly modifies those terms.

The court shall provide copies of the presentence investigation report to the parties at least fourteen days before sentencing. If the report is not provided within this period, a party may move for a continuance. The court shall grant such motion unless it finds good cause to proceed immediately.

Before imposing sentence, the court shall address the defendant personally and afford the defendant an opportunity to speak in his or her own behalf. If the defendant declines to speak, the court may proceed with sentencing. This requirement applies regardless of whether counsel has already made a statement on the defendant’s behalf.

In misdemeanor trials with eight jurors, the court shall reduce the panel to six immediately after verdict submission but before deliberation begins. If an alternate substitutes for a seated juror during deliberations, the court must instruct the jury that the substitute assumes all prior proceedings and evidence as if present from the start, without further explanation or comment on the substitution.

On motion of an indigent defendant seeking appellate counsel in a district court misdemeanor appeal with suspended sentence, the appointing authority shall designate counsel within ten days after receipt of the motion. The motion must be filed within twenty-one days after entry of the judgment or order appealed from. Failure to file timely constitutes waiver of right to appointed counsel on appeal.

The special juvenile criminal rules apply to any person charged with an offense who was under eighteen years of age at the time of the alleged offense, regardless of whether jurisdiction originated in family division or circuit court. These rules govern all proceedings involving such persons unless otherwise provided by law. The court shall ensure strict compliance with these procedural safeguards throughout the adjudication process.

Before enforcing an order requiring a parent to pay for appointed counsel in a juvenile prosecution transferred to adult court, the court shall conduct a hearing on the parent’s ability to pay. The parent must be given notice and an opportunity to be heard. Payment obligations shall not exceed the parent’s reasonable financial capacity as determined by the court after considering income, assets, and other support responsibilities.

Upon arraignment on a complaint and warrant, the court shall set the preliminary examination within fourteen days. Any prior adjournment granted in the family division shall not extend this period unless good cause is shown and the interests of justice require it. The prosecution must file a motion for extension before expiration of the initial fourteen-day period.

If the magistrate finds no probable cause for the qualifying offense but finds probable cause for a lesser offense, the juvenile shall be bound over to circuit court on the lesser charge. The prosecutor shall provide the transcript of the preliminary examination at public expense. The juvenile is not required to pay for the transcript regardless of the finding on the qualifying offense.

The court shall consider the minor’s degree of participation in planning and carrying out the offense when determining whether to impose adult sentence or juvenile probation with state wardship. This determination must be made at the hearing, weighing all relevant factors including the nature of the crime and the minor’s culpability.

Upon conviction for a new felony offense, the court shall commit the defendant to the Department of Corrections if the defendant was previously placed on juvenile probation after being charged as an adult. The court may not impose alternative sentencing or further probationary supervision unless specifically authorized by statute. Commitment is mandatory and immediate upon entry of judgment, subject only to statutory exceptions regarding mental health or competency proceedings.

The facility shall notify the court at least ninety days before the juvenile’s nineteenth birthday. The clerk shall issue notice to the prosecutor and parents at least thirty days before the hearing. On motion of a party, the court may extend or shorten these time periods for good cause shown. Failure to provide timely notice does not invalidate the proceeding if actual notice is received.

The court shall conduct a final review of the juvenile’s status no later than sixty days prior to the expiration of the commitment period. Upon such review, if the juvenile remains committed, the court may impose an adult sentence for the underlying offense, provided that notice has been given and the juvenile has had an opportunity to be heard regarding the proposed disposition.

The circuit court may exercise jurisdiction over an appeal from a district court judgment if the time for filing a notice of appeal has expired, provided the moving party demonstrates good cause for the delay. The motion must be filed within one year after the expiration of the time for appeal. The court shall grant relief only if prejudice to the opposing party is not shown and justice requires it.

A party appealing from district court to circuit court must file a transcript of proceedings within 21 days after filing the notice of appeal. If transcription is unavailable or unduly burdensome, the appellant may move for leave to proceed without a transcript. The court shall grant leave if satisfied that the record is sufficient for review and that denial would cause undue hardship.

An appellee must file an answer within fourteen days after service of the application for leave to appeal. The trial court may extend the time for cause shown. Failure to file an answer constitutes a waiver of the right to be heard on the application, unless the court orders otherwise.

An opposing party must file an opposition within fourteen days after service of the application. The opposition shall contain a statement of facts, arguments, and citations to authority in the same form as a brief on appeal. Each party’s counsel must sign every pleading. Failure to comply may result in denial of the application without prejudice.

A party seeking to cross-appeal from a judgment or order must file a notice of appeal within twenty-one days after the filing of the first notice of appeal. If a motion is pending in the trial court when the first notice of appeal is filed, the period for filing a cross-notice of appeal runs from the entry of the order disposing of the last such motion.

If a main appeal is dismissed while a cross-appeal remains pending, the cross-appellant must file the reporter’s certificate within ten days after entry of the order dismissing the main appeal. If no transcript is required, the cross-appellant shall file a statement to that effect within the same period. Failure to comply constitutes waiver of the right to proceed on the cross-appeal.

On appeal from district court to circuit court, the circuit court may modify any bond or undertaking required by the district court. The circuit judge shall determine the amount and conditions of security necessary to ensure compliance with the judgment. This authority applies regardless of whether the modification is requested by a party or initiated sua sponte by the court during the pendency of the appeal.

To stay enforcement of a district court money judgment pending appeal to circuit court, the appellant must file a bond or other security with the clerk. The amount must equal the judgment plus accrued interest, costs, and sanctions. The court may set a different amount on motion for good cause shown. Failure to file sufficient security within ten days after entry of judgment waives the right to stay enforcement.

A stay bond must recite the title of the case, the names of all parties, and the specific judgment or order sought to be stayed. It shall state the amount awarded below and the interest accrued. The bond must be executed by a surety approved by the court and filed within 10 days after filing the notice of appeal, unless the court orders otherwise for good cause shown.

On appeal from district court to circuit court, the reviewing court’s powers are limited to those expressly conferred by these rules. The court may not remand for additional proof or permit amendment of pleadings to add new grounds unless specifically authorized herein. Any action beyond the scope of these appellate provisions is prohibited, regardless of practices in other courts.

The court may dismiss an appeal for failure to comply with filing requirements. Before dismissal, the court shall notify the party of the deficiency and afford a reasonable time to cure. If the party fails to correct the defect within ten days after notice, the court shall dismiss the appeal. The court may extend this period for good cause shown.

A prevailing party must file a bill of costs within 21 days after entry of judgment or order disposing of the appeal. If a party fails to file a bill of costs within this period, the court may, on motion and for good cause shown, extend the time for filing. Failure to file a bill of costs within the prescribed time constitutes a waiver of the right to recover costs.

An appeal from an administrative agency’s final decision shall be commenced by filing a notice of appeal with the circuit court clerk within forty-two days after the agency mails its decision. The notice must specify the party appealing and the relief sought. No other pleading is required to initiate the appeal. The record on appeal consists of the agency proceedings.

If the enabling act is silent regarding security, the circuit court shall determine the amount of bond or other security required to stay the agency order. The court shall also approve the sufficiency of sureties. A party seeking the stay must post such security within ten days after the court’s determination, unless the court orders otherwise for good cause shown. Failure to post security results in dissolution of the stay.

A paper is filed when delivered to the clerk of the court for entry on the docket. Delivery by mail or electronic filing constitutes filing upon receipt by the clerk, not upon dispatch. The clerk shall stamp each document with the date and time of receipt. If a party fails to comply with formatting requirements, the clerk may reject the filing or accept it subject to correction within three days.

A party seeking review of an order denying a postjudgment motion affecting parental rights or custody must file a notice of appeal within twenty-one days after entry of the order. Leave to appeal is not required for such orders. Failure to timely file constitutes a waiver of appellate rights unless good cause is shown.

A party seeking review must file a claim of appeal with the Court of Appeals within twenty-one days after entry of the judgment or order sought to be reviewed. The claim shall state the grounds for relief and identify the parties. No other papers are required at the time of filing the claim, unless otherwise ordered by the court on motion showing good cause.

A party appealing as of right from an order adjudicating guardianship over an individual with a mental disability shall designate that status on the face of the notice of appeal. This designation requirement applies exclusively to appeals involving child custody determinations or orders declaring a statute unconstitutional, and does not extend to other probate matters.

A motion for leave to file a notice of appeal out of time shall be filed within six months after the expiration of the period prescribed by MCR 7.205(B) or (C). The Court of Appeals may grant leave if good cause is shown. Failure to file within this six-month period results in a permanent bar to appellate review, and the trial court’s judgment becomes final.

A party seeking to revive a dismissed appeal must file a delayed application within ten days of the dismissal order. The application shall address the identical lower court judgment or order previously appealed. Failure to target the same order renders the application void for lack of jurisdiction. The Court of Appeals may grant leave to proceed only upon showing good cause for the initial failure to perfect the appeal.

The applicant shall file with the application for leave to appeal a certified copy of the judgment and sentence, and the transcript of the proceedings at which the plea was entered and the sentence imposed. If other proceedings are relevant to the issues raised in the application, the applicant shall also file transcripts of those proceedings.

Upon granting leave to appeal, the Court of Appeals shall issue an order directing the appellant to file a docketing statement within fourteen days after entry of the order. No claim of appeal is required when leave to appeal is granted. Failure to file the docketing statement within the prescribed time constitutes a waiver of the right to appeal and may result in dismissal of the appeal.

On motion of a party showing good cause, the Court of Appeals may expedite consideration of an application for leave to appeal. A motion for expedited consideration must be filed with the clerk and served on all parties within seven days after filing the application. The court shall rule on the motion promptly.

The respondent shall file an answer within twenty-one days after service of the petition. The answer must respond to each allegation. A party may attach affidavits, exhibits, or other evidence in support of the answer. Failure to file an answer constitutes a waiver of objections to the relief sought.

On initial review, the court may deny relief or grant argument. If the court grants argument, it shall issue an order setting briefing dates. A party must file its brief within 21 days after service of the order, unless the court orders otherwise. Failure to timely file constitutes waiver of argument. The court retains discretion to dismiss the petition for failure to prosecute.

Upon filing of the answer, the Clerk shall randomly assign three judges to the panel. Assignment occurs within ten days after service of the answer. A judge may recuse himself or herself on motion for cause shown. No further assignment is required unless a vacancy arises. The assigned panel retains jurisdiction until final disposition.

If genuine issues of material fact exist, the Court of Appeals shall remand the case to the trial court for evidentiary proceedings. The trial court must receive testimony and make findings of fact within sixty days after remand. The appellate court may not take direct testimony or resolve factual disputes de novo. Parties must file proposed findings within ten days after the conclusion of evidence.

In an action challenging legislative apportionment, the respondent shall file a brief within thirty days after service of the complaint. The brief must conform to MCR 7.212(C) regarding form and content, unless the Court of Appeals orders otherwise on motion or sua sponte. Failure to comply may result in sanctions or dismissal of the appeal.

The bond shall obligate the appellant to pay the judgment amount, plus interest and costs, if the appeal is dismissed or affirmed. This obligation remains in effect until final disposition of the appeal. Failure to satisfy the judgment within thirty days after affirmance authorizes immediate execution against the surety without further court order.

If no verbatim record exists, the trial court shall prepare a statement of the evidence or proceedings. A party may file objections within fourteen days after filing. The trial court shall resolve objections and certify the statement. The certified statement constitutes the record on appeal. The clerk shall transmit the certified statement to the appellate court with the record.

Upon filing the transcript, the reporter shall immediately notify the clerk of the Court of Appeals and all parties. The reporter must file a certificate of service with the trial court confirming such notification. Failure to provide timely notice may result in sanctions or dismissal of the appeal for lack of prosecution.

Upon filing of a motion to withdraw as appellate counsel pursuant to MCR 6.004(D)(2), the defendant shall file an answer within fourteen days after service of the motion. Failure to file an answer constitutes consent to the relief requested. The court may extend this time for good cause shown.

On remand, the trial court must grant a new trial if it previously stated an intention to do so. The Court of Appeals may not reverse such a determination unless the trial court abused its discretion in making the prior statement or the statement was legally insufficient to bind the lower court.

Upon affirmance or dismissal of an appeal, the appellant’s counsel shall provide the client with a copy of the transcript within fourteen days. Counsel must file a certificate of service with the court confirming delivery. Failure to comply constitutes grounds for disciplinary action. The court may extend this period for good cause shown on motion.

A respondent’s brief must be served within 21 days after service of the appellant’s brief. The parties may not stipulate to extend this time limit without leave of court. On motion, the Court of Appeals may extend the time for good cause shown. Failure to serve a brief within the prescribed time constitutes waiver of appellate rights unless excused by the court.

Unless the court orders otherwise, the filing of a motion does not extend the time for filing a brief. If a dispositive motion is pending when a brief is due, the party must file the brief within the prescribed time. The court may stay briefing upon motion showing good cause, but such stay is discretionary and not automatic.

A party seeking to exceed page limits must file a motion for leave within fourteen days after filing the brief. If the court denies the motion, the deadline for filing the brief is extended by seven days. The court may grant or deny the motion without prejudice to other deadlines.

An appellant’s brief must contain a jurisdictional statement identifying the date of filing the notice of appeal or other document conferring jurisdiction. If the appeal arises from a criminal proceeding, the statement shall also identify the date of sentencing. Failure to include this information constitutes grounds for dismissal of the appeal unless cured within ten days after service of the brief.

In a criminal appeal attacking sentence, counsel for appellant must file with the brief a certified copy of the judgment of conviction and sentence, unless previously filed. If the record on appeal is incomplete, counsel shall request supplementation from the trial court within ten days after filing the notice of appeal. Failure to comply may result in dismissal.

A nonparty filing an amicus curiae brief shall disclose any party or person who paid for the brief’s preparation or submission. This disclosure must appear on the cover page of the brief. Failure to include this statement constitutes grounds for striking the brief. The court may impose sanctions for noncompliance with this requirement.

The appellant shall file an appendix within fourteen days after filing the notice of appeal. If the record is available electronically, the parties may stipulate to omit the appendix. In such cases, citations must include specific page numbers or document identifiers from the electronic docket. Failure to comply with these requirements constitutes waiver of error.

The appellant shall file the appendix in portable document format (PDF). The PDF must be text-searchable through optical character recognition. Internal bookmarks or navigation aids are not required unless ordered by the court on motion for good cause shown. Failure to comply with these formatting requirements may result in rejection of the filing.

The appellant shall file an appendix containing the relevant parts of the record, including pleadings, orders, and exhibits relied upon by either party. The appendix must include a table of contents listing each item with its page number. Parties may stipulate to omit items not essential to resolution of the issues on appeal.

The parties may file a joint appendix by agreement. If filed jointly, the appendix shall be filed with the appellant’s brief within fourteen days after service of the notice of appeal. Failure to file a joint appendix requires each party to file a separate appendix in accordance with this rule. The court may order otherwise on motion for good cause shown.

A party may move for publication of an unpublished opinion within twenty-one days after entry of the order disposing of the appeal. The motion shall state specific reasons why the opinion should be published.
