The court shall grant the motion only if it determines that the opinion establishes a new rule of law, applies an existing rule to a significantly different factual situation, or conflicts with another published decision.

A decision of the Court of Appeals becomes final and operative upon the expiration of the time for filing a petition for leave to appeal, or upon the denial of such a petition by the Supreme Court. If a timely petition is filed, the decision remains stayed until the Supreme Court disposes of the petition or remands the case.

Upon voting to seat a conflict panel, the Court of Appeals shall immediately notify the Supreme Court in writing. The notification must specify the identity of the assigned judges and the case caption. This report is mandatory regardless of whether the vote was unanimous or divided. No further action by the parties is required to trigger this reporting obligation.

On motion of any party, the Court of Appeals may award damages for frivolous appeal if it finds the appeal was filed solely to delay proceedings or harass. The court shall assess costs against the appellant and counsel. A party seeking such relief must file a motion within ten days after entry of judgment. The court may impose sanctions upon finding bad faith or lack of merit.

If no transcript is ordered within thirty days after filing notice of appeal, the clerk shall notify the appellant. If the appellant fails to order the transcript or file a brief within sixty days of that notice, the court may dismiss the appeal on motion of any party or sua sponte. The presiding judge shall enter the order of dismissal.

A party seeking costs must file an itemized bill with the clerk within fourteen days after entry of the final disposition. If a motion for reconsideration is filed, the time to file the bill runs from the date of the order denying the motion. Failure to file within this period constitutes a waiver of the right to recover costs.

Upon receipt of the Commission’s recommendation for removal, the Supreme Court shall convene to consider the matter. The Court must determine whether probable cause exists to believe the judge has committed misconduct warranting removal. If probable cause is found, the Court shall appoint a special master or proceed directly to trial. No further motion or leave of court is required to initiate this review.

A party may petition the Supreme Court for leave to appeal from a published opinion of the Court of Appeals if that opinion conflicts with another published opinion of the Court of Appeals on the same question of law. The petition must be filed within twenty-one days after entry of the Court of Appeals’ order disposing of the case.

If the Court of Appeals remands a case for further proceedings, the time to file a notice of appeal to the Supreme Court runs from the entry of the order denying a motion for reconsideration or other post-remand relief, if such motion is filed within the time prescribed by rule. Otherwise, the time runs from the entry of the remand order.

A party may appeal from an order entered after remand. The appeal is limited to issues arising from the post-remand proceedings, unless the Court of Appeals expressly reserved jurisdiction over prior claims. A petition for leave to appeal must be filed within twenty-one days after entry of the order.

A party may file a reply brief within seven days after service of the answer. The reply must be served on all parties. No more than ten copies shall be filed with the clerk, unless the court orders otherwise. A reply addressing matters not raised in the answer requires leave of court. Failure to comply with these requirements constitutes grounds for striking the reply.

A nonparty seeking to file an amicus curiae brief in support of an application for leave to appeal must first obtain written consent from all parties or permission of the Court on motion. If permission is granted, the amicus brief shall be filed within ten days after entry of the order granting permission, unless the Court specifies a different time period.

Upon denial of leave to appeal, the judgment or order of the Court of Appeals becomes final. A party may enforce the judgment immediately upon receipt of notice of the Supreme Court’s denial. No stay is in effect unless expressly ordered by the Supreme Court or the Court of Appeals prior to the denial.

In an original action challenging presidential election certification, the Court shall issue its final order no later than six days before the electors meet to cast their votes. An order issued after this deadline is not binding on state officials or federal authorities for purposes of determining certified results. The Court may extend this period only upon a showing of extraordinary circumstances that do not delay the electoral process.

A party seeking to cross-appeal must file a notice within fourteen days after the opposing party files an application for leave to appeal. Failure to file within this period constitutes a waiver of the right to cross-appeal. The court may not extend this time limit, nor shall it grant relief from the deadline for any reason, including excusable neglect or inadvertence.

On motion by the Governor, the Supreme Court may certify a controlling public-law question from a pending trial court action. Upon certification, the trial court shall stay proceedings until the Supreme Court resolves the certified question. The lower court must transmit the record within ten days of the order. Parties shall file briefs on the merits within thirty days thereafter.

A party may file a motion for rehearing within 21 days after entry of the order denying leave to appeal. The motion shall state with particularity the points of law or fact believed to have been overlooked or misapprehended. If the motion is denied, no further application for review may be filed in this Court regarding the same matter.

A party who is both an appellee and a cross-appellant may file a single brief addressing both appeals. The brief must be filed within forty-two days after entry of the order granting leave to appeal or filing the notice of appeal, whichever occurs later. The brief shall contain separate sections for the response and the cross-appeal, clearly designated as such.

On motion or sua sponte, the court may impose sanctions for frivolous conduct, including misrepresentation of the record in briefs. Sanctions shall be imposed only after notice and an opportunity to respond. The court may order payment of reasonable attorney fees and costs incurred as a result of such improper conduct.

If no record is filed within sixty days after notice of appeal, the clerk shall dismiss the appeal. A party may move to reinstate the appeal within thirty days after dismissal. The court shall grant the motion if good cause is shown for the failure to file the record. Failure to move within thirty days results in final dismissal.

On motion of all parties, the Court may dismiss an appeal pending before it. The motion must state that the case has been settled or otherwise resolved. If filed within seven days of oral argument, the moving party shall pay any costs incurred by the opposing party in preparing for argument. The Clerk shall enter judgment dismissing the appeal upon approval.

A party unable to pay fees may file an application for leave to proceed without prepayment. The application shall be filed with the required documents. No fee is charged for the application. If the court denies the application, the party must pay the original filing fee within ten days of denial or the action shall be dismissed for failure to prosecute.

The administrative rules in this chapter apply to all trial courts, including circuit, district, and probate courts. Each court shall adopt local rules consistent with these provisions within ninety days of adoption. The Chief Justice may issue orders necessary to implement uniform administration across all judicial districts. Compliance is mandatory for all judicial officers and court personnel.

A party may record proceedings using personal equipment only with prior court approval. Upon request, the court shall permit such recording if it does not disrupt the hearing. All recordings remain the property of the party and may be used for case preparation. The court may impose conditions to protect confidentiality or prevent prejudice. Unauthorized dissemination is prohibited unless ordered by the court.

The chief judge shall be selected by majority vote of the active judges of the court. No formal application is required. Selection must occur within thirty days after a vacancy arises or upon expiration of the term. If no selection is made within that period, the senior active judge shall serve as chief judge until a successor is chosen.

The chief judge of each circuit court shall establish the hours of operation and determine the minimum number of judges and staff required to be present during those hours. These determinations must ensure adequate access to justice and efficient administration of judicial business. The chief judge may modify these requirements upon finding that existing arrangements are insufficient or inefficient, subject to approval by the Administrative Office of the Courts.

The chief judge shall report to the state court administrator each quarter any felony case pending disposition for more than one year after bindover. The report must include the case number, defendant name, and date of bindover. This reporting requirement applies only to cases where no final judgment has been entered within twelve months of the binding over order.

The chief judge must report to the state court administrator all misdemeanor and ordinance cases pending for more than one hundred eighty days. This period is computed from the date of arrest or issuance of a summons. Cases pending less than one hundred eighty days need not be listed on the quarterly criminal caseload report, provided they are actively being processed by the court.

A judge attending judicial education programs outside the state judicial conference must obtain prior approval from the Chief Justice or designee. Such attendance shall count against the annual twenty-day allotment for professional development. Requests for approval must be submitted in writing at least thirty days before the program begins, detailing the curriculum and relevance to judicial duties.

Upon recusal or disqualification, the chief judge shall reassign the case without stating cause. The successor judge is selected by lot or rotation. Within three days of assignment, the clerk must serve written notice on all parties identifying the new judge and setting a preliminary conference date. No motion to vacate the reassignment order is permitted unless fraud or conflict of interest is alleged.

A court shall solicit comments from the local bar association before adopting a local rule. The court must transmit the proposed rule, together with any comments received, to the Administrative Office of the Courts within thirty days after adoption. The rule becomes effective only upon approval by the Supreme Court or the Chief Justice, as applicable.

During trial, spectators in the gallery shall not communicate with any witness while that witness is testifying. Such communication includes electronic messaging, texting, or other digital transmission. The court may impose additional restrictions on electronic device usage to preserve decorum and prevent interference with judicial proceedings. Violations constitute contempt of court.

On motion to close the courtroom, the court must find that closure is no broader than necessary to protect the identified interest. The order shall specify the duration of closure and limit it strictly to the testimony requiring exclusion. General closures are prohibited. The court must make specific findings on the record demonstrating that less restrictive alternatives were considered and rejected before ordering any closure.

Any person adversely affected by an order closing proceedings may file a motion to reopen within seven days of entry. If the court denies the motion, the movant may seek immediate appellate review pursuant to MCR 7.213(A). The application for leave must be filed with the trial court within fourteen days of denial and served on all parties.

The plaintiff must designate one primary case type upon filing the initial pleading. Where multiple causes of action exist, the court may assign additional codes. This designation governs all subsequent filings unless amended by order. The clerk shall maintain the primary code for docketing purposes. Parties may request reclassification on motion showing good cause.

A clerk shall accept for filing any document that is properly prepared and filed in accordance with these rules. A clerk may reject a filing only if the document fails to comply with formatting requirements, lacks required fees, or is otherwise legally insufficient on its face. The clerk must provide written notice of rejection stating specific grounds.

When an item is filed electronically and enters the chronological record without manual entry by a deputy clerk, the system shall automatically assign the initials of the filing party or attorney to that entry. This automated designation serves as the official record of receipt and supersedes any requirement for clerical initialing in such instances.

Upon migration of legacy scanned filings to the statewide case management system, the clerk shall maintain a thirty-day hold on public access. After thirty days, unless sealed by court order or exempted by statute, the filings shall be immediately available for public inspection and copying through the electronic filing system.

A clerk shall charge fees for copies of records at rates established by the State Court Administrative Office. Fees shall not include capital costs, depreciation, or amortization of imaging systems or equipment. Charges must reflect only direct reproduction expenses. Any fee schedule incorporating indirect overhead costs is prohibited and subject to immediate correction upon motion by any party.

An attorney’s fee award against an insurer under statute shall not be applied toward the statutory percentage limitation on contingency fees. Fees derived from such statutory awards are excluded from the calculation of total compensation for purposes of determining compliance with maximum allowable percentages. The court shall treat statutory fee recoveries as separate from client-funded contingency arrangements when assessing fee reasonableness and statutory caps.

The affidavit of the sponsoring attorney must state that the out-of-state lawyer has not appeared in more than five Michigan cases within the preceding twenty-four months, or explain why such limitation does not apply. The affidavit shall also certify that the applicant is authorized to practice law in another jurisdiction and is of good standing.

A party’s participation in an administrative complaint regarding interpreter competence shall not constitute a waiver of the right to raise such issues in the underlying proceeding or on appeal. Preservation of error requires timely objection at trial. Failure to object constitutes waiver, regardless of any parallel administrative proceedings. The court may consider administrative findings as evidence of incompetence.

The clerk of the court shall maintain current contact information for all magistrates assigned to the district. Upon request by a party or upon the magistrate’s removal from service, the clerk shall promptly provide such details to the requesting party or successor magistrate, ensuring continuity of proceedings and proper notification of judicial assignments within the district.

Upon final disposition of the proceeding, the clerk shall retain the original will in the court file for five years. After such period, unless the will is under seal or otherwise ordered retained by the court, the clerk may destroy the document in accordance with state records retention schedules. The clerk shall provide notice to interested parties before destruction if required by statute.

The current disciplinary rules govern all pending proceedings and apply to conduct occurring prior to their effective date. These rules shall be construed to effectuate their general purpose to make uniform the practice and procedure under the rules, promote simplicity in administration, and secure just determination. No right, privilege, or duty heretofore acquired shall be impaired by this adoption.

A respondent must file an answer to a grievance within twenty-one days after service of the complaint. The answer shall specifically deny each allegation or admit it in part. General denials are insufficient. Arguments based on industry custom, prevalence of conduct among other attorneys, or absence of prior disciplinary action are not valid defenses and shall be disregarded by the court in determining liability.

The Chief Justice shall appoint the chair of the Attorney Grievance Commission for a term of two years. No person may serve more than two consecutive terms as chair. The appointment must be made within thirty days following the expiration of the preceding chair’s term or upon vacancy. Reappointment is prohibited if the individual has completed two full consecutive terms.

The Chief Judge of the Attorney Grievance Commission shall appoint and remove the Executive Director. Removal shall occur only for cause, including incompetence, misconduct, or neglect of duty. No removal may be effected without prior written notice and a reasonable opportunity to respond. The Chief Judge must file a certificate of appointment or removal with the Clerk of the Supreme Court within ten days of the action.

Upon learning of a pending confidential grievance involving himself, a panelist shall immediately disclose this fact to the parties and withdraw from service. The disclosure must occur within three days of such knowledge. Failure to disclose constitutes grounds for disqualification upon motion by any party. The presiding officer may extend this time for good cause shown.

Upon determining that a grievance lacks merit or is frivolous, the administrator may dismiss it without referral to the commission. The administrator shall notify the respondent lawyer in writing of the dismissal within ten days. The notice must state the reasons for dismissal and advise the lawyer of the right to request reinstatement of the grievance by filing a written motion with the commission within twenty days of receipt.

Within fourteen days after service of the order accepting the admonition, a respondent may file a motion to withdraw acceptance or object to the sanction. If no such motion is filed within the prescribed time, the grievance commission shall certify the matter as closed and transmit the final record to the Board of Commissioners of Grievances for entry on the public register.

The Administrator shall produce all exhibits to the respondent within ten days after service of the notice of hearing. Any exhibit not produced within this period is inadmissible, unless the panel finds good cause for late production. Exhibits supplied during the week immediately preceding the hearing are presumptively excluded from evidence.

The respondent may offer to surrender the license to practice law in exchange for an agreed sanction. Such agreement is ineffective unless accepted by the Attorney Grievance Commission and approved by the Supreme Court. No stipulation regarding discipline shall bind the parties or the court without such acceptance and approval.

The written stipulation must specify the proposed discipline based on respondent’s admissions and prior history. It need not cite external benchmarks. The grievance administrator shall review the stipulation for consistency with disciplinary standards. If consistent, the administrator may approve the sanction without further proceedings. Approval requires that the proposed discipline adequately addresses the misconduct and serves the interests of justice and public protection.

Upon denial of a negotiated discipline proposal, the panel shall issue a written order specifying the reasons for rejection. A party may file an amended proposal addressing those deficiencies within fourteen days of service. The panel shall consider the amended proposal without further hearing unless good cause is shown. Failure to file within the prescribed time constitutes waiver of the right to submit revised terms.

Upon dismissal of charges against a referee by the Tenure Commission, the Commission shall immediately notify the referee and the Chief Justice. The notice must state that the charges are dismissed and specify the effective date. No further action is required unless the Commission determines additional proceedings are necessary under applicable law or rule.

Within twenty-one days after filing of the report, a party may file objections to findings or recommendations. Failure to object constitutes waiver. The court shall review de novo any objectioned findings. Unobjected findings are adopted unless clearly erroneous. The court retains authority to accept, reject, or modify recommendations.

Upon receipt of final discipline from another jurisdiction, the Board shall issue notice to the respondent. The out-of-state misconduct finding is conclusive unless the respondent proves by clear and convincing evidence that the other proceeding lacked due process or resulted in fundamentally unfair results. The respondent must file a motion contesting reciprocal discipline within twenty-one days of service.

On motion, the court may appoint an independent examiner. The report shall be disclosed to all parties prior to trial. If any party objects to the examiner’s testimony, the court may exclude the report unless the examiner is called as a witness. The party seeking admission of the report shall bear the cost of securing the examiner’s attendance and compensation for testimony.

On motion by the State Bar or sua sponte, the court may order an attorney respondent to submit to a psychological or medical evaluation regarding fitness to practice. If the respondent refuses to comply with such an order within fourteen days, the court shall deem the allegations of unfitness admitted and may impose sanctions, including immediate suspension from the practice of law, pending further proceedings.

The panel may impose additional conditions of probation beyond those specified in this rule when necessary to protect the public or ensure compliance. Such conditions shall be reasonable, related to the misconduct, and clearly stated in the order. The respondent must comply with all imposed conditions during the probationary period. Failure to comply constitutes grounds for immediate suspension.

Probation shall not exceed five years. The court may extend probation upon finding good cause. An attorney may move for early termination after serving two years. The court shall grant the motion if the attorney demonstrates sustained compliance and rehabilitation. Extensions require notice to the Board of Commissioners of Character and Fitness.

An attorney inactive due to disability may petition for reinstatement every twelve months. The petitioner must prove current competence and fitness to practice law. If inactive for more than five years, the petitioner shall also demonstrate completion of continuing legal education requirements prescribed by the Board of Commissioners of State Bar Rules.

An attorney suspended for twelve months must file an affidavit of compliance with the Administrator not earlier than thirty days before the suspension expires. Upon receipt of a complete affidavit, the Administrator shall restore the attorney’s license automatically unless the Administrator finds probable cause that the attorney has failed to comply with the suspension order or other disciplinary requirements.

The petitioner shall file a sworn statement detailing all financial accounts held or co-signed during the preceding five years. This statement must specify account ownership, balances, and transaction history. Failure to disclose such information constitutes grounds for denial of reinstatement. The court may require additional documentation upon motion by any party within ten days of filing.

The petitioner shall pay the grievance administrator’s reasonable fees and expenses upon reinstatement. These costs cover investigation, hearing preparation, and administrative processing distinct from board expenses. Payment must be made within thirty days of the order granting reinstatement. Failure to pay constitutes grounds for vacating the reinstatement order. The court may enforce payment through contempt proceedings.

The panel shall schedule a hearing within thirty days of receiving the administrator’s findings. A party may move for a determination based solely on affidavits and records. Unless the panel orders otherwise, personal appearance is not required. The panel may require oral argument or in-person testimony if necessary to resolve material factual disputes regarding eligibility for reinstatement.

Upon closure of a grievance without formal charges, the respondent attorney may request disclosure of the outcome. The Board shall grant such request unless public release would violate applicable confidentiality laws or compromise ongoing investigations. Disclosure must occur within thirty days of the final order. The court retains discretion to seal records if necessary to protect judicial integrity.

Upon mailing notice of nonpayment, the attorney’s license is suspended immediately. No hearing is required for suspension. The attorney may petition the court to reinstate the license by proposing a payment plan. If the court approves the plan and the attorney complies, the suspension is stayed pending full satisfaction of the assessed amount.

The parties must execute a written agreement submitting the fee dispute to arbitration before filing. Upon completion of arbitration, the arbitrator shall file the award with the clerk of the court having jurisdiction over the grievance. The award is final and binding unless vacated by the court within thirty days of filing for fraud, corruption, or misconduct.

Upon final disposition of a complaint resulting in removal, suspension, or censure, the Commission may assess against the respondent judge all reasonable expenses incurred in investigating and prosecuting the complaint. The assessment shall be made within thirty days after entry of the final order. Payment must be made within sixty days unless otherwise ordered by the Commission.

A member of the Commission on Judicial Tenure who is the subject of an investigation shall recuse herself from all proceedings concerning that investigation. She must abstain from voting, deliberating, or participating in any decision regarding her own tenure. Failure to recuse renders any action taken by the Commission in that matter void.

Upon receipt of a complaint against a judicial candidate within sixty days of an election, the Commission shall not conduct a public hearing or issue a final determination until after the election concludes. The Commission may, however, take immediate interim action to protect the integrity of the judiciary if necessary. All other investigative proceedings shall remain confidential and suspended pending the resolution of the election.

If the executive director prosecutes the charges, the director shall appoint an independent special counsel to advise the commission. The special counsel shall possess full authority to investigate, prepare documents, and present evidence. This appointment must occur within ten days of the director’s decision to prosecute. The special counsel reports directly to the commission, ensuring impartiality in proceedings where the executive director serves as prosecutor.

The respondent judge shall file a written answer within twenty-one days after service of the complaint. The answer must respond to each allegation specifically. Failure to deny an allegation constitutes an admission thereof. The court may grant leave to amend or supplement the answer on motion for good cause shown. Pleading standards applicable in civil actions do not govern judicial misconduct proceedings.

The neutral arbitrator shall notify the parties of the hearing date at least fourteen days in advance. The arbitrator shall rule on any dispositive motion within ten days after submission of briefs or oral argument, whichever is later. Failure to comply with these time limits does not invalidate the proceedings unless a party demonstrates substantial prejudice.

Upon receipt of the hearing officer’s report, the Commission shall notify each party of the right to file written exceptions within fourteen days. No oral argument is permitted unless the Commission, on its own motion or upon a party’s request demonstrating good cause, orders otherwise. Failure to file timely exceptions constitutes a waiver of the right to challenge the findings.

Upon signing a negotiated resolution, the Commission shall submit its recommendation to the Court. The recommendation must address any prior disciplinary history relevant to the current matter. Unless otherwise ordered by the Court for good cause shown, the recommendation and all supporting materials regarding the judge’s prior discipline shall be filed as public records within ten days of execution.

Upon appeal to the Supreme Court, the Commission shall designate counsel to represent it. The attorney who prosecuted the complaint before the Commission shall not serve as counsel on the appeal unless expressly authorized by the Commission. All briefs and filings must comply with Supreme Court rules regarding judicial tenure proceedings.

In tenure proceedings, service of a formal complaint upon a sitting judge shall be made by certified mail, return receipt requested, addressed to the judge’s chambers. Personal service is prohibited. Proof of service must be filed with the Court Administrator within ten days after mailing. Failure to comply with this method of service renders the filing null and void.

The Commission shall adopt written policies governing the retention, storage, and disposition of records related to judicial complaints. These policies must specify the duration for which each record type is maintained and the procedures for its secure destruction or transfer upon expiration. The Commission shall implement these policies within ninety days of adoption and shall make them publicly available upon request.

A person who files a complaint with the judicial tenure body, or an attorney assisting in its preparation, is immune from civil liability for acts performed in good faith within the scope of their duties. This immunity applies regardless of the complaint’s merit. No court shall entertain a civil action against such persons arising from these activities.

The Commission shall develop and administer continuing legal education programs for judges regarding judicial ethics and conduct. The Commission may publish guidelines, advisory opinions, and other materials to assist judges in complying with the Code of Judicial Conduct. These educational activities shall be conducted at times and places designated by the Commission, subject to available resources and approval by the Supreme Court.

Upon the death or sudden incapacity of a solo practitioner, any member of the practitioner’s firm may substitute as counsel. The substituting attorney must file a notice of substitution within fourteen days. The court may require proof of authority. All pending proceedings shall continue without interruption unless the court orders otherwise on motion for good cause shown.

Upon a partner’s inability to practice, remaining attorneys may continue representation without court appointment if clients consent in writing. Such consent must be filed with the clerk within thirty days of the disability. Absent written consent, the court shall appoint counsel upon motion. Failure to file consent or secure appointment mandates withdrawal from all pending matters.

A lawyer winding down the practice of a suspended attorney who is adverse to a former client in an unrelated matter shall notify that client within fourteen days of becoming aware of the conflict. The notice must advise the client of the right to retain new counsel and request the return of files, unless disclosure is prohibited by other rules or law.

Fees awarded to an interim administrator constitute a lien on the suspended lawyer’s trust accounts and firm assets. The lien attaches as of the date of the court order appointing the administrator. The administrator shall file proof of claim within thirty days of the fee award. The court may enforce the lien against any property held by the firm or in the control of the administrator to satisfy the judgment.

An attorney appointed to wind down an inactive lawyer’s practice shall maintain professional liability insurance covering services rendered during the appointment. Coverage must remain in effect until the court discharges the appointee. Failure to maintain such insurance constitutes grounds for immediate removal and may result in disciplinary sanctions. The appointee shall file proof of coverage with the clerk within thirty days of appointment.

Upon assuming responsibility for winding down an attorney’s practice, a successor attorney may handle open matters only after providing the client with written notice specifying the identity of the successor, the scope of representation, and any change in fee arrangements. Such notice must be delivered within ten days of assumption of duties. The client shall have thirty days to object to the continuation of representation by the successor attorney.

These rules shall be known as the Michigan Court Rules. In citing a rule, the abbreviation MCR shall be used. A specific rule shall be cited by its number, for example, MCR 2.111. References to these rules in pleadings and other documents may use the abbreviation MCR.

If a conflict exists between a general rule and a rule specifically applicable to a particular court or proceeding, the specific rule governs. In the absence of a specific rule, the general rule applies. This provision ensures that specialized procedural requirements take precedence over broad directives when addressing unique judicial contexts or case types within the Michigan court system.

The court shall maintain electronic case records including metadata, system-generated entries, and audit trails created by the e-filing software. These data points constitute official case records for all purposes. Parties may inspect such records upon request. The clerk shall preserve these records in accordance with state archival standards.

If an order is entered orally on the record, the court shall promptly prepare and sign the written order. A party may submit a proposed order to the court within seven days after oral entry. The clerk shall file the signed order immediately upon receipt. Failure to file does not invalidate the order if it was correctly stated on the record.

A party seeking redaction of sensitive data from a trial exhibit shall file a motion specifying the items to be blacked out. No filing fee is required for such motions. The court may grant the request if it finds that public disclosure would cause substantial harm outweighing the public interest in access. The moving party must serve the motion on all other parties at least seven days before the hearing date.

On motion to seal exhibits, the court clerk shall immediately restrict public access to the designated materials pending judicial determination. The clerk must segregate such documents from the general file and maintain them under seal until the court enters an order granting or denying the motion. No party shall inspect sealed materials without prior leave of court.

Upon entry of an order restricting public access to specific exhibits, the clerk shall immediately seal those designated materials. All other filings within the same document that were not specifically identified in the court’s directive shall remain part of the public record and accessible to any person requesting inspection, unless otherwise ordered by the court or prohibited by law.

If the court orders that private contact information be redacted from the public file, the order shall designate an alternative address or telephone number for service of process and other communications. This substitute contact point must remain effective throughout the pendency of the action unless the court modifies the order upon a showing of good cause.

A clerk shall accept filings that omit social security numbers required by local forms. The court may not sanction a party or refuse acceptance solely because such information was left blank. Compliance with federal privacy mandates supersedes local form requirements. Parties must provide other identifying information as prescribed by rule.
